PASSPORTS AMENDMENT BILL (NO 2)
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I move, That  the Passports
Amendment Bill (No 2) be now read a first time. At the appropriate moment I intend to
move that the bill be referred to the Government Administration Committee for
consideration and that the committee report finally to the House on or before 30 October
2015. This is a concise but important bill that will ultimately help many New Zealand
citizens. It contains measures that are designed to make passport services more
convenient for travellers, and it modernises the Passports Act 1992 to reflect  the
increasingly electronic nature of passport services.
The main feature of this bill is that it increases the validity period of the adult New
Zealand passport to 10 years. This addresses a common concern raised about the current
validity period of the New Zealand passport in that when matched by passports issued
by comparable countries our passport is valid for a shorter period. This was an issue
considered carefully by the Government Administration Committee last year before it
recommended a review of the passport validity period. New Zealanders are well known
for their love of travel and, being as geographically isolated as we are, the passport is an
essential document for many people for both business and holiday purposes. It is simply
inconvenient having to renew a passport more frequently than in many other countries.
The validity period was originally reduced from 10 years to 5 years in 2005 against a
background of security concerns at that time. The New Zealand passport was not
4572 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015
considered then to be a sufficiently secure document, so in order to reduce its
attractiveness to counterfeiters, there was a need to ensure that the passport was in
circulation for a limited time and that its security features were improved. Reducing the
validity period addressed some of those risks, and the launch of the e -passport, which
introduced an electronic chip containing biometric information about the passport
holder, enhanced the passport’s security.
Since 2005 there has been significant investment in passport se curity, both for the
security of the book itself and of the issuing processes. The book has been updated a
number of times and now contains many effective security features alongside the
biometric chip. Other countries have updated the security in their pa ssports in recent
years and have also been confident enough to increase the validity periods of their
passports to provide greater convenience to travellers. I believe New Zealand should
now do the same.
We have a passport that is considered to be amongst  the best in the world. However,
security challenges still exist. The international security situation is constantly changing
and remains volatile. Therefore, in considering a change to the passport validity period,
the Government has sought to ensure that  passport security would not be compromised.
That is why in August last year I announced an independent review of New Zealand’s
passport security settings. That review and subsequent work has carefully considered
the relevant issues and involved the border  and law enforcement agencies in that
process. We are now confident that the security risks involved in moving to a longer
validity period can be mitigated.
This change to the passport validity period applies only to adult passports, which are
issued to i ndividuals who are at least 16 years of age. Children’s passports will still
have a 5 -year validity period, in line with international convention, which recognises
that younger people’s appearances change more quickly.
In addition to changing the maximum validity period for adult passports, the bill will
also change the validity periods of other travel documents. This includes extending the
validity period of refugee travel documents from 2 years to 5 years. That brings them in
line with the length of the residency period required before refugees can apply for New
Zealand citizenship and obtain a New Zealand passport.
The bill reduces the maximum validity period of certificates of identity from 4 years
to 2 years. These travel documents are issued only to non- New Zealand citizens who
cannot get travel documents from their own countries. As we may not have full access
to these individuals’ identity information, the majority of certificates of identity are
issued for 1 year only, so it is therefore appropriat e to amend the Act to reflect this
reality and the greater security concerns around those travel documents.
In addition to changing the validity period of travel documents, other changes in this
bill are designed to ensure that New Zealand’s passport services are supported by up-to-
date legislation. The bill does this by removing outdated provisions that are inconsistent
with modern security and operational practice. For security reasons, passports and other
travel documents that expire or need to be change d because their visa pages are full are
now replaced by completely new documents. The original documents are not amended
in any way. Therefore, the current provisions in the Act, which enable the expiry dates
of passports to be extended and additional visa  pages to be inserted, are redundant and
are being removed.
In a similar vein, the bill also removes references in the Passports Act to the
reissuing of travel documents. This change reflects the fact that new travel documents
with updated identity details for the document holder replace any previous document.
The bill also provides clear legislative authority for best practice document security. For
instance, clauses in the bill authorise the permanent invalidation of passports and other
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4573
travel documents that have been reported lost or stolen, and this helps prevent the use of
such passports for criminal purposes.
Other clauses refine provisions in the Act that already enable the recall and
cancellation of passports for specified reasons. These amendments in the bill provide for
the travel document database to be flagged when passports have been recalled or
cancelled. This information is then shared with border control agencies quickly under
existing arrangements.
Finally, the bill gives extraterritorial application to the offence of false
representation. This change aims to reduce the risk of the online passport application
service being misused by individuals who are based overseas or who apply to the
Department of Internal Affairs’ London or Sydney offices with false information.
To conclude, I believe it is important that the operational practices of this world-class
Government service are supported by modern legislation. The majority of the
amendments in the bill are of a relatively minor and technical nature, or they simply
update the Act to reflect computerised processes. In that respect, the bill will ensure that
the passport service continues to operate effectively to help New Zealand citizens living
all over the world, and that appropriate safeguards preventing the misuse of the service
are put in place and maintained.
Importantly, the bill will ensure that New Zealanders will benefit from the
convenience of a longer passport validity period. I believe that the House should
therefore get this bill moving through the select committee process and enacted as soon
as possible, and it is with considerable pleasur e that I now commend the bill to the
House.

items.speaker: ADRIAN RURAWHE
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise to
speak to the first reading of the Passports Amendment Bill (No 2). I would describe the
New Zealand passport as a taonga, actually. When we are travelling overseas, the New
Zealand passport allows us to visit 170 other countries without a visa. The New Zealand
passport has a very high standard and is recognised around the wor ld as having a very
high standard of quality attached to it. So the New Zealand passport is valued by every
single New Zealander, I believe, who has one. New Zealanders do not like 5 -year
passports. Despite the fact that in 2005 there was a real need to ha ve such a passport,
New Zealanders have never liked it and have actively sought a longer period of validity.
Increasing it to 10 years was Labour Party policy last year. We had a campaign to raise
the validity of a passport to 10 years from 5 years. More t han 15,000 people signed a
petition to that effect, and we made that our policy. So it is really good to see that this
bill has finally made it to the House to increase the validity of New Zealand passports
from 5 years to 10 years. That is certainly somet hing that the Labour Party supports. It
was, in fact, our policy, and it is good to see that the Government has finally caught up.
In talking about this amendment bill, I want to also touch on a number of other
things, particularly an issue that will be important to New Zealanders, and that is the
cost of making applications. Over the past 5 years, due to timing issues, I have actually
had to renew my passport three times in that period. One of the things that New
Zealanders will be thinking about —and I re fer to “Regulatory impact statement:
Passport validity period” and its executive summary’s point No. 6. It reads: “The
decision on whether to remain with a cost -recovery model or provide Crown revenue to
limit fee rises is, in our view, a decision involvin g political trade -offs that should be
made by Cabinet.” Never a truer word was written. The actual cost of processing a
passport, apparently, is around $400. It has been recorded that in order to, I guess, make
this more palatable for New Zealanders to acc ept, the Minister has said that it would be
set at around $180. We know that leading into this period, the cost of processing the
passports in the last few years has been subsidised from an accumulated fund, which is
4574 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015
now exhausted. I understand that there would need to be additional funds to subsidise
the processing of passports moving forward over the next 5 years and beyond.
I also want to make a point that in transitioning from a 5 -year passport to a 10 -year
passport, in around 2020 there would be possi bly, or most probably, a surplus of staff.
Logic tells me that me that if you are extending the validity of passports to 10 years then
there will be fewer passports to be renewed over a period of time—a transitional period
of up to 5 years out. That is cer tainly, on this side of the House, an issue that we would
take particular interest in, and we look forward to the select committee process so that
we can examine fully these kinds of issues.
As the Minister of Internal Affairs pointed out, there are a num ber of technical
changes in this bill. I am particularly interested in the online issue. I am sure we will
have good and robust debate and discussions in the select committee over that issue. I
am going to try to compare what I think —because I am not absolutely certain that there
is a need to remove that option. I am told that technology advances in the power of the
computer double every year, so we might want to look more closely. As a comparison I
will say this: as I understand it, last year the select co mmittee, in its examination of the
passport issue, came to the conclusion that having biometric data within passports was
more likely to have reduced the falsifying or counterfeiting of passports than the 5- year
validity period. I would also suggest that m aybe technology, as it advances, could be
available to address those concerns about having online renewal of passports. I think
that the online applications for new passports might be a separate issue, but I do look
forward to having a discussion in the se lect committee stage around those particular
clauses.
The Minister in charge of this when it becomes an Act will have the ability also to
record or to note warnings on files, travel documents, and passports. I think we need to
carefully examine that as well to make sure. We are seeing other similar legislation go
through the House and I think that it would be important for us to ensure that that is
used appropriately and that New Zealanders always have the ability to get home. We
have discussed other bills and Acts in this House that traverse that issue and I think that
within the Government Administration Committee, it is one of the areas also that I
would be paying particular interest to.
I go back to my original comments about the 5- year validity period increasing to 10
years. I certainly do wonder why it has taken so long. I am pleased that it has finally
arrived here, but I am bound to say that it is another example of the Government being
out of touch with New Zealand families, because they have been talking about this issue
for quite some time. For the Government to only now  be dealing with this particular
issue—at this stage of the Government’s 7 years on the benches opposite —I think that
maybe this is political poll policy, reacting to what New Zealanders want, albeit very
slowly and albeit with some real doubts about some of the things in this bill. The
Labour Party will be supporting this bill’s referral to a select committee. Thank you
very much. Kia ora.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: I rise in support of the Passports
Amendment Bill (No 2), and it is a true pleasure to take this short call because this is
going to be a very popular move. We have all wanted this for a while, but in response to
the member opposite Adrian Rurawhe, I think it is important to outline why it was the
case that our 10 -year period of validity for passports was reduced to 5 years. That was
done, of course, on the back of the 9/11 attacks in the States, which were horrifying
events and really did change the world landscape with regard to terror. Since then, we
have seen such horrific events through Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant and other
terror groups, so it is very important for us to take our se curity seriously. As passports
are our prime form of identification, we need to make sure that our passport holds its
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4575
integrity and that we deter counterfeiters from preying on a passport, as the member
opposite did identify for himself. He said that our passport is well respected and valued
overseas. So, as part of that, the Government has looked at biometrics, bringing in place
a chip to store biometric information about the passport holder in the passport, but, of
course, reducing the term was one way to  deter counterfeiters from preying on our
passport.
So that was the reason, but of course since then we have secured the passport. The
security is now good. We are quite pleased with where we have got to, and now it is
time to increase the term again, and  that will be well received. There is nothing worse
than having to turn around and fill out more forms after a short time to reapply for
travel. New Zealand is a nation of travellers. In fact, 77 percent of us hold passports,
and being, as the Minister sai d, geographically isolated as a country, the tradition has
always been that Kiwis will fly, and we head off and do our OE, or overseas experience.
I am no exception to that, of course, and I needed a passport to do that, and I guess that
was when I realised the full value of travelling on a Kiwi passport. It is well respected,
our country is well respected overseas, and it helps the ease of travelling through
Europe. So of course this is going to be a popular bill. It is going to be well received,
but I cer tainly look forward to the process as we progress this through the select
committee.
The other thing about this amendment bill is that it is not going to extend the validity
period for children. Obviously, children’s appearances change too rapidly. I have  got a
couple of children myself. I see how fast they grow. They sprout up like mushrooms, so
security-wise we simply cannot issue them a 10 -year passport. You would take a photo
and just a couple of days later it just would not reflect who they were, so i t is important
that we maintain that difference. It is important for security, and I think that mums and
dads will understand that exemption in respect of maintaining our security but having to
update passports for their young ones.
I want to touch on the  online system, because of course it is a target of this
Government under our Better Public Services target to have most—77 percent, in fact—
of our interactions with the Government online. The online system of applying for
passports has been well received,  and the take-up has been very good. That is going to
improve interactions with the Government. The system, again, is secure and will help
people through the process of applying for a passport and getting that as a good and
secure form of identification.
So it is with pleasure that I partake in this first reading of this bill. I think it will be
something that is well received by the public. It is refreshing, to say the least, to try to
keep down and minimise paperwork. But, at the same time, the public should be
heartened that our passport is in a good space, is secure, and obviously is still well
respected around the world. Thank you.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Kia or a, Mr Assistant
Speaker. I rise to take a call on the Passports Amendment Bill (No 2). Over the last
couple of days, and again later in the House today, I have been and will be speaking a
bit about passports and about the quality of citizenship. Passports are, as my colleague
Mr Rurawhe says, a taonga. They are important to us, and they do differentiate us from
other people around the world. They are well sought after by those unscrupulous people
who would take our passports off us, because having a New Zea land passport allows us
to travel to many countries of the world where other passports may not take those
passport-holders. We do support this bill going to the select committee, and there are a
few components of this bill that I am hopeful the select committee will spend some time
reviewing and refining and coming back to us with some answers for.
4576 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015
The most significant part of this bill is the validity period —moving that from 5 years
to 10 years. As my colleague has already said, that really has come about  by public
pressure—New Zealanders not really enjoying the shortened 5 -year period of their
passports. We are great travellers, being right down here at the end of the world. We do
a lot of travelling, and the renewal period is quite prescriptive being at 5 years.
The issue around the cost is interesting. The Minister of Internal Affairs has made
various statements in the public arena about the cost being set at $180 and this
reflecting, really, the cost savings over the period of time of moving out the va lidity
period from 5 to 10 years. That is a very interesting point, and I do want to just pick up
on something that I read, a statement from the Minister that came out in the Taranaki
Daily News  a couple of days ago, which shows that Cabinet papers reveal that the
Government will need to front an extra $200 million to double the validity period to
actually cover the costs of the passport. The actual cost of the passport sits at around
$400. I think this is really interesting because Treasury did say to the Department of
Internal Affairs that it did not want this decision made based on financial reasons. But
Mr Dunne is in favour of subsidising the passport in order to keep it affordable as a
public good. Although I understand that the ability to have a passport and to travel is an
important right for a New Zealander, it does seem like an issue that should be discussed
at the select committee, because it does seem at odds with Treasury recommendations.
Also a very good point was made that the child’s passport  stays at 5 years, because,
yes, it is true that children’s appearances do change, and a period of 10 years would not
be appropriate for them. But the 10- year validity period throws into the mix another
issue and that is around the issue of technology and how quickly technology does move.
In terms of our passport with its chip, we were one of the first countries to move to the
passport with a chip, which makes it easier to move through borders as the process is
much quicker, but it also does beg a question about technology. Ten years is a long time
in the technological world, the modern age. It is a long time, and technology will
change quickly over that time. The ability to potentially counterfeit passports or to find
ways to replicate chips in passports in that 10 years is a distinct possibility.
One of the concerns I have that I hope the select committee will pick up on is that
there will not be the need to see the physical passport in order to cancel it. You can do
so electronically on the database. I am  concerned for a couple of reasons. What
concerns me is that mistakes do happen, and it would seem like a useful checking
process to have the physical passport in front of you before you actually cancelled that
passport. We know from other discussions in t his House that databases, including the
databases of the Government, are not always entirely secure, and it is a possibility that
databases can be hacked or manipulated and people may have their passports cancelled
when that is not actually required. That also brings into question the ability for Kiwis to
return home should their passports be invalidated incorrectly. This bill also provides for
the extraterritorial application of the offence of false application, which I thought was
an interesting phrase. W hat that means is that when you apply to an overseas New
Zealand passport office if your application is falsely made it is now an offence for that
application to be made at an overseas passport office.
I have referred to the cost of the 10 -year passports, but I found it really interesting
that one of the concerns is around the issue of identity documents. When it comes to
foreign nationals who do not have appropriate identity documents, we are looking to
reduce the length of validity of identity documents that an overseas national without
appropriate identity documents can have down to a period of 1 year. This is an issue that
has come up in my electorate a couple of times in the last couple of years. There have
been people from Somalia who have identity do cuments that are not considered valid in
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4577
a number of jurisdictions, and they are finding it very difficult to have any ability to
travel—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I apologise for the
member’s colleague—it is very disorderly, Mr Lees-Galloway.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Thank you. Just to reiterate, I was talking about the identity
documents for certain groups of people. We are moving in this bill to reduce the period
of time for which we will provide identity documents for people who find it difficult to
have their own national identity documents recognised by New Zealand. I was referring
to Somali people. I know there is some issue with them being able to obtain appropriate
documents through the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.
I also just want to pick up on a point that the previous speaker spoke to—that 70
percent of the interactions with the Government are to go online. Although on the face
of it that sounds like a very useful process, it does also flag the fact that there are
barriers for those people  who do not have access to online facilities. What mechanisms
are to be in place for people who cannot use computers, do not have access to
computers, may not be able to afford the internet, or cannot access free internet because
of remote locations? It does call into question why we would have such a high reliance
on our interactions being online. There is also, again, the issue of security around online
interactions and the ability to hack into and manipulate those systems. So, just in
conclusion, I say t hat I look forward to the work the select committee will do on this
issue, and I hope that it will be able to address some of the concerns I have raised.
Thank you.

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: I rise in support of the first reading of the Passports
Amendment Bill (No 2). It is a great pleasure to be able to stand here and be giving the
public what they have requested—a bill that will return a New Zealand passport to a
validity period of 10 years, and one that supports New Zealanders’ desire to be, and
history of being, adventurous and global explorers. In doing so it is important to note
that we will not be compromising the security or indeed the international reputation of
our passport. It will contain the latest technology to protect passport holders from
identity fraud. It will ensure that our passport holders can access as many countries
tomorrow without a visa as they can today—a number that is around 170.
It is important to reflect on the fact that the reputation of New Zealand’s passport is
extraordinarily high. We are in fact the eighth most desirable passport in the world in
terms of the number of countries we can access without an entry visa, and that comes
from a study done by global advisory fir m Arton Capital. It may not surprise anyone in
New Zealand to know that as eighth in the world we are ahead of Australia, and in fact
with the performance post the global financial crisis of this National- led Government, it
will not surprise any Australian s that we are ahead of them now too. But we do indeed
have a very strong reputation for the quality, security, and robustness of processes
around our identity documents.
But that reputation also is something of a magnet for criminals, fraudsters, people
who realise that if they can get hold of a New Zealand passport —if they can counterfeit
one, if they can repurpose one —then they have an advantage of themselves or other
people perhaps being able to access the borders of other countries that much more
easily. I just have a quote here from a Massey University Centre for Defence and
Security Studies lecturer Rhys Ball. He noted that “The Kiwi passport helps reduce an
individual’s profile. It is looked upon as a non- threatening travel document originating
in a country with a robust processing system.”
But it is worth noting that although we are very strong and robust in our processes,
we are not immune from fraudulent activity. In the period from 2010 to 2014 over
11,000 New Zealand passports were stolen and over 42,000 were lost. In fact, even in
4578 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015
just one case in 2009, Roderick Robinson used Rex Smith’s passport to flee to Portugal
in that year. So we must remain ever vigilant. When we look at that, it is the reason why
we moved to the state that we are currently in with a 5-year validity period.
I just want to recap that a little because I think the history of where we have come
from is important in understanding why we can now make a change without
compromising security. So it was in the early 2000s —in 2002—when the Department
of Internal Affairs advi sed the Minister of a rising number of attacks on New Zealand
passports and a shift from crimes of opportunity to crimes of intent with sophisticated
forgery and counterfeiting. There was also the new US legislation for homeland security
that demanded mach ine-readable passports with biometric identifiers. Non- compliance
with that would have seen us lose our visa -waiver status, which would have required
Kiwis travelling to the States to visit the US consulate in Auckland in person and to pay
visa fees.
On t op of that, in 2003 there was a review on border security, particularly around
counter-terrorism threats and measures. So a bill was introduced and given to the
Government Administration Committee in 2004. After hearing submissions and
deliberating, it reported back that it recommended that passport validity be reduced to 5
years. It noted that the longer a passport has been in circulation, the greater the chance
that its security features will become outdated and easily altered or successfully
duplicated. Its view was that security and international reputation outweighed the
inconvenience of a shorter validity period.
It is with great pleasure that our officials will tell us now —and that we in this
Parliament are now debating it and saying that it is possible —that we can now take a
position where we can react to changes in the world, where we have a very, very robust
and secure passport, and that we can, in fact, look to return to a much longer validity
period of 10 years without compromising the security of our people’s identities or
risking our international reputation. It is going to be a very, very good debate in the
select committee. I look forward to that and I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I rise to take the first call for the Greens on the
Passports Amendment Bill (No 2). I think when we are looking at the bill and its
introduction it is important to trace back to where the inspiration for this policy change
came from. I bel ieve that it was from a petition launched by Kyle Lockwood. In his
interview in the Sunday Star -Times he said that he was inspired to create the petition
after he saw a really upset mother with her son at Melbourne airport who could not fly
because her passport had less than 6 months left on it, so it was about to become invalid.
It is important that we acknowledge the democratic process and that it was a petition
that ultimately led to this bill coming to the House and that it was a campaign that did
that. Although the democratic process can move really slowly, we really do need to
celebrate the fact that an ordinary New Zealander was listened to in the halls of power
and we are, hopefully, changing policy as a result. I guess from our point of view this i s
a good partial application of one of the principles of our founding charter for the Green
Party, which is appropriate decision- making. That means that decisions are made
directly, at the appropriate level, by those affected. Although the people who are
affected did not directly get to decide, I am glad that we have listened to the voice of
Kyle Lockwood.
We have been supporting that campaign for 10- year passports throughout the
process. My colleague Mojo Mathers agreed with the recommendation from the
Government Administration Committee to review the current system with a view to
extending it once that petition came to the select committee. We support this move for a
variety of reasons. The policy of 10- year passports will save ordinary New Zealanders
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4579
the hassle, the stress, and the time -consuming nature of applying for a new passport as
well as saving money.
There has been some discussion about what it costs. The current cost of the 5- year
passport is $134.50, or $26.90 a year. The proposed fee of $180 for the 10-year passport
works out to be just $18.00 a year. This proposal also brings us into line with
international standards. Much of the European Union, most of the Americas, most of
Asia, and even our cousins in Australia have 10- year passports. I thi nk it is fair to
acknowledge the evidence from the Department of Internal Affairs that was presented
during the select committee inquiry. I have to say that it ultimately concluded its
evidence by saying that it considers a 10 -year validity period acceptab le. But it had
serious concerns about reintroducing 10- year passports because it feared that it would
encourage criminal organisations to invest in counterfeiting New Zealand passports, and
I think that is a fair concern.
That is, I guess, why we are so disappointed that this National Government has been
investing fewer resources in public safety through the police that would counter that.
Yesterday my colleague David Clendon released figures that show that spending on the
Police budget has fallen by 5.7 p ercent, which means that there is less public safety
happening, and certainly less investigation. This is, sadly, emblematic of the National
Government’s chronic under-investment in public services, and that is a point that was
reinforced in a report released on 8 June by the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions,
saying that our health system, for example, was $1 billion worse off than 6 years ago,
which works out to be about $220 per New Zealander.
The fact that the department’s submission identified that the change from 5 years to
10 years could lead to a revenue problem further reinforces my point that under this
National-led Government our public services are scrambling to penny -pinch the pockets
of hard-working New Zealanders. The Government has basical ly been fiscally reckless
by giving tax cuts to the very wealthy on their top incomes.
We are assured by the evidence given at the Government Administration
Committee’s review of the passport validity period that biometric passports  reduce the
risks of counterfeiting and identity fraud to such a degree that the validity period could
be safely extended —and that is a direct quote. However, we do have some concerns.
They arise from the findings of Simon Murdoch’s passport security review, as laid out
in the r egulatory impact statement for this bill, where he concludes by saying that
investment would be necessary to reduce the risks of moving to a 10- year validity
period. That is why we would much prefer that the added security of biometric
passports was supplemented by adequate funding of public safety. We need to restore
that 5.7 percent to the police. Although technology can be a wonderful thing, it is no
substitute for an adequately funded public service. We cannot, and should not, skimp on
funding our core public services. An investment approach is absolutely crucial for our
country’s security.
There are other measures in this bill that we support, such as better provisions for
cancellation, and usage of our travel documents database. In the 21 st century it should
not be necessary for a modern Government department to physically cancel a document
that needs to be sent and received sometimes from half a world away. Also, this data
move will save us money and time. Despite many disagreements with my colleagues
across the House on many, many issues, I am happy and we are happy to be working
with them on this issue to make a change that was spurred on by an ordinary New
Zealander. It is fantastic to see democracy in action when it actually works. Thank you.

items.speaker: CLAYTON MITCHELL
items.text: I stand to take a call for New Zealand First in
the first reading of the Passports Amendment Bill (No 2).

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Very strong opinions.
4580 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015

items.speaker: CLAYTON MITCHELL
items.text: And already, David Seymour, you are into it. I would
like to start by simply saying: David, if you throw a party, and you are the only
person—

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Standing Orders  require the
member to refer to another member by his full name, not only his Christian name.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That is actually not quite
accurate, but the Speakers’ rulings do require that, and the member, I am sure, will react
much more appropriately to future interjections.

items.speaker: CLAYTON MITCHELL
items.text: Absolutely. So let me finish what I am saying, Mr
Seymour of the David variety. At the end of the day if you throw a party, and you are
the only person who shows up at that party, are you actually throwing a party or are you
just a person by yourself at home alone —because it is a lot of noise from a very, very
small corner over there.
I would like to add that I have been as busy  as a bee with a bum full of honey in the
Beehive today, and there has been a little bit of a lack of preparedness for today’s
delivery. But I dare say I think that just about every single New Zealander could stand
up and speak to this piece of legislation, because finally we have got a little bit of
common sense. I would also like to say this —and I bet you that this compliment does
not come across very often to the honourable member Peter Dunne —for the simple
reason that I commend him for fighting hard to get the costs of passports down when
Cabinet was originally coming out with a fee of around $225, and for bringing that fee
down to $180. So I would like to congratulate him on fighting a good fight for New
Zealanders; however, I think that there is still more of a fight that needs to be had.
Although New Zealand First strongly supports this bill —in fact, back in 2012 the Rt
Hon Winston Peters spoke to this matter for the first time, and New Zealand First was
the first party to say that this was absurd. The reality of cutting back passports from 10
years to 5 years when the vast majority of the world—the Western World that was
supposedly affected by the terror attacks —kept their passports at 10 years, for me, was
that it was an opportunity for this Governme nt to collect revenue, to put some money in
the coffers, and it was at the expense of everyday Kiwis.
Sarah Dowie also mentioned the 77 percent of Kiwis who have passports. That is
fantastic. We are a flightless bird and we do like to travel the world. I myself have had
many passports and travelled the world too, but we should be making it affordable for
100 percent of Kiwis to be able to do that. Travel internationally at the moment is
probably the cheapest it has ever been, and we should not be excluding  any New
Zealander from being able to afford that right. Denise Roche said that the cost of
passports over a 10- year period is going to be reduced by nearly $100 over that period.
But if you think about it, the actual cost of putting a passport together is  the same—it
does not matter whether you are doing it for 5 years or 10 years. So in actual fact there
is no cost saving. We should be able to bring the cost of passports back even more than

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Oh, fixed and variable costs, mate.

items.speaker: CLAYTON MITCHELL
items.text: And if you would let the grown- ups just speak for a
moment, Mr Seymour, we might give you some sort of positive thinking and some
practical, sensible, and innovative ideas. If we are just throwing a little bi t of a sling out
here, the reality is that at the moment, I think, there are 20- odd pages in a passport. If
we cut back the number of pages in a passport —because let us be honest, back in the
1990s when I was doing some prolific travelling you used to have to ask for countries to
stamp your passport, and even after 10 years you could not actually fill up all the pages
in your passport. It was almost like you would wear it as a badge of honour—how many
different countries you went to when you were travelling  around Europe. By simply
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4581
looking at things practically we might actually be able to reduce the cost of those
passports by reducing the number of pages that are in them, and that might be brought
out in the select committee.
The second point I would like to bring your attention to is how quickly this
Government can react —with the recent retrospective legislation it has put through and
backdated that ripped the $1,000 kick- start contribution off the table. So we know that
this Government when it is in actio n can get things done. That piece of legislation did
not suit the vast majority of New Zealanders, but this piece of legislation does. We have
been getting a lot of correspondence and I am sure that Labour has been getting it and
that National has been get ting it. The Greens have certainly been getting it as well. We
have, in New Zealand First, people writing to us to ask why this piece of legislation is
taking so long to come through. It should not take this amount of time —until 1 January
2016—to get this through. If we have made a decision as a political movement, and it
looks like we have got full support across the table, I for one would be happy to debate
this in urgency and take it right through to the end stages to push this through.
There will be Su pplementary Order Papers, but the reality is that there are people
here right now in this country waiting to put in their applications for their passports.
They are wanting to travel, but they cannot, and they are going to be locked into a 5 -
year passport deal. Right now it looks like we are seriously making a move forward for
the betterment of New Zealand, so why cannot this go into urgency? I urge you to
consider that and put that to the House for consideration.
There are some serious concerns from New Zealand First with regard to a media
report that was sent out last week, on 9 June, about the potential doubling up—$400 by
2021—for those costs of passports. The cost and the time issue are certainly the most
fundamental issues that we have to keep up with the play on. We understand about the
modernising of the Passports Act 1992 and about the 16- year-olds who get only 5- year
passports. We understand that. I think that is a sensible, pragmatic solution. I have got
young children myself, and goodness me, they  change. From the week that I start
Parliament to the week that I get home they look different. I can understand that that is
in line with the rest of the world, so we also support that.
I would also like to say, just to finish things off —because, again, I could waffle on
and take up 10 minutes of everybody’s precious time back home —that I think the
message is clear out there that we are behind in this. The piece of legislation putting
passports back to a 5- year passport was not from the National Government, as was
suggested; it was actually done by the Labour Government. I think that move was a
little bit too quick off the hip and I think we should have stuck with those 10- year
passports. Now it is coming down to getting those costs down and actually making it
affordable for New Zealanders to travel.
I am concerned that the cost of travelling is being increased with new legislation, the
travel tax, that has been put through—$16 out; $6 com ing back. A young family with
four or five family members wanting to pop across the Ditch to Australia for a week is
now up for $100-odd. Putting in the cost of the passport, we need to do what we can to
get these flightless Kiwi birds out on their planes and travelling around the rest of the
world. It is a great world to see, but when you are out there you realise what a
wonderful country we live in, and it certainly does make you appreciate it a lot more.
Thank you.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: This week was a little unusual for me. I
have had the pleasure of sitting on the Government Administration Committee, and now
I have got the privilege of speaking on a bill that is going to the Government
Administration Committee.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Moving up in the world.
4582 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I must be, as the whip says, moving up in the world. I have been
promoted.
But, anyway, during the Budget debate on the border processing arrivals and
departures levy we learnt how many people were coming and going from New Zealand
now—some 5.2 million per year —and of those, about 2.5 million are New Zealanders,
so, clearly, thos e 2.5 million need to have a New Zealand passport. It shows the very
high demand for New Zealand passports. In fact, we know that 77 percent of all New
Zealanders have a New Zealand passport.
Interestingly, passports are not always used for travel. Most e lectorate MPs will
know that through their electorate offices they will get a lot of people coming in
complaining about the fact that they have got to find some form of ID. If they do not
have a driver’s licence or, indeed, a firearms licence or something like that, then a
passport is often the only form of ID they can effectively use. There are people who do
have a passport but never use it for travel, so passports are a broader thing than just
being used for travel.
Just to go into the background of this  bill, the terrorism acts of 2001, in my view,
were a good reason for the Government of the day to change—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Tell us about sheep passports.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: Well, we have clearly had a lot of discussion on sheep passports
this week. It proved my point, actually—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Oh, God—ha, ha!

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: Well, you are clearly on my side on that. Mr Assistant Speaker, I
have been distracted.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am having trouble with the
relevance of it.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: But the reason we reduced the terms of those passports was, of
course, for security reasons around identity security and around the ability to track
changes in behaviour of people from time to time, and new technology has now given
the Government the opportunity and the confidence, I guess, to extend the period of
passport eligibility to 10 years, which, as the previous speakers have noted, will make a
difference to the cost of a passport and will certainly make a difference to the amount of
hassle one has in getting a passport. In fact, like one of the previous speakers, I have
had to get three passports in the last 5 ye ars because I inadvertently dumped one of my
passports as it came in the post from the Passports Office —so the online passport
system was not exactly clever.
But, surprising as it may seem, I think this is a Government that cares, listens to New
Zealanders, and reacts appropriately. Although we may feel that Governments are slow
to react, I think we also need to realise that Governments are creating legislation and
law for the long term. I think it is pretty essential that something as important as a
passport gives us the opportunity to be sure that we are on very solid ground before we
change the law around passports and find ways of issuing them.
As many people have said, it is a privilege to hold a passport for a start, and this new
legislation will mak e it easier for the authorities to remove a passport. They will not
have to have it in hand. It is done merely by the click of a button on a computer or a
phone. It will be easier to get a passport. It will be easier to take a passport away. I think
the wh ole process will be improved by the introduction of the Passports Amendment
Bill (No 2). That is my short contribution to this bill, and I wish it all the best as it goes
into the select committee process.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: This is a 5-minute call from the Green Party. I call Mojo
Mathers.
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4583

items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: I rise to take a call on the Passports Amendment Bill
(No 2). The Green Party supports this bill and, in part icular, we support the provision to
extend the term of adult passports to 10 years. I was on the Government Administration
Committee last year, which considered the petition that has triggered this legislation. I
just want to acknowledge the very high cali bre and quality of the information that was
presented in support of this petition. It was incredibly well researched and was backed
up with lots of evidence about what is happening around the world to show that it is an
exceptionally reasonable request to go back to a 10-year term for adult passports.
The petition was presented by Kyle Lockwood and was signed by more than 15,000
New Zealanders, but the public discussion in the media shows that this is just the tip of
the iceberg and that this was something of extreme concern to many New Zealanders —
the cost, the hassle, and the stress involved in having to renew their passports every 5
years. In fact, the 5- year term means that passports are, in effect, only really valid for
4½ years for a lot of travel overs eas, because of the requirement to have a passport that
is valid for 6 months. I think it is really encouraging to see an ordinary New Zealander
making such good use of the democratic process, bringing a case to the select
committee and being heard by the select committee, so that we were compelled to make
a recommendation in favour of the request. It has been absolutely fantastic to see the
Government responding to that and now bringing legislation to the House to address
that concern.
One of the key point s that were made by the petitioners in favour of the extension
was the fact that most of New Zealand’s trading partners have 10 -year passports —
whether we are talking about Australia, the US, China, the UK, and so on. It is even
more compelling because of t he fact that New Zealand is on the inter -governmental
group that developed this passport —this practice. Four of the five countries on that
committee—that is, the other four —all issue 10 -year passports, and they are Australia,
Canada, the UK, and the US. It  was starting to look and feel like New Zealand was
being overly paranoid about passport security, when all of our trading partners and the
people on the committee that is actually considering this passport practice have 10- year
passports. Why are we, a sm all country down here in the Pacific, being so excessively
paranoid about passport security? In addition, the International Civil Aviation
Organization has also recommended 10- year passports. So, again, how can we decide
that 5 years is the best practice? I think it is just silly.
Of course, the public also moved that with the incredible strives in biometric
information, we can either address or mitigate a lot of the security concerns. We are
never going to have 100 percent security around passports, but what we can look at is
what a reasonable level of security around passports is. I feel very confident that we can
address these security concerns at the select committee when the bill comes to the select
committee. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5-minute call. I call David Seymour.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: An earlier speaker said that he found it a
great pleasure to speak on this bill, and he said it with great conviction. It was possibly
more a reflection of the member than the bill, but it is important that we get this
technical adjustment made. I cannot help but respond to a few earlier speakers. There
was one from the Labour Party who said that it was a policy issue as to whether
passports should be funded by user -pays or general taxation. Only the modern Labour
Party would seriously contemplate taxing the working class to pay for a good that is
entirely private in its benefit—entirely private in its benefit —and used by people who
can afford to leave the country. But that is a sad commentary on the current state of the
Labour Party members, who have forgotten whom they represent and where they are.
4584 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015
I thought perhaps I should also respond to the earnest member from New Zealand
First, only to say that I believe he is improving in his speaking and may become a very
good parliamentarian in due course. I wonder, members, whether I should try to explain
to him the difference between fixed and variable cost s, but he has got the professor—oh
no, he does not. Perhaps I should try to explain that the reason it can cost more per unit
to produce a smaller number of passports is that indeed some costs are fixed and others
are variable.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: How much did it cost for David’s garage?

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I think that was a private arrangement, Mr Lees -Galloway. I
would like to speak on behalf of some constituents I have heard from who have told me
that they find themselves  in the difficult position of being eligible to renew their
passport between now —or at least between August 2014, when this change was first
announced—and the time when they will be able to get a 10- year passport. These
people, “the 1¼ years people”, find themselves requiring another 5- year passport, and
they are missing out on the benefit of this bill.
If you think about it, there is a 5- year term for passports, so in 1¼ years around 30
percent, nearly a third, of all passport holders will be caught in the delay between the
announcement of this change and the change coming into effect. Indeed, it was
announced first in August 2014. It was announced again in April 2015, and it was
announced again in May 2015. As one of my constituents wrote, this has been
announced more times than the coming of Christ. And how many times does the
Government impose a simila rly complex —or, indeed, much more complex —change,
which is ultimately a change in a price and date, upon small businesses and across New
Zealanders and their households, and expect them to adapt much more rapidly to far
more complex changes with so little notice?
This is a worthwhile consideration for anybody who thinks about the impact that we
in this House can have upon people when we make regulations, when we raise taxes,
and when we provide services in a certain way. So often, the regulations and the A cts in
this House have a disproportionate cost imposed on people out there, and it is very
important that we are always mindful of the impact that the Government, with its
coercive powers and its very powerful legislative instruments, can have on the welfa re
of ordinary New Zealanders. So with those few considerations in mind, I, like Brett
Hudson, take great pleasure in the idea that we will soon again have 10- year
passports—a much more efficient outcome— and I commend this bill to the House.
Thank you.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I rise to take a call on the Passports Amendment Bill
(No 2) in its first reading and, obviously, commend it as it goes through to the
Government Administration Committee. Like m y honoured colleague over here Ian
McKelvie, I have not sat on that select committee, but I believe that the work of the
select committee will be important in discussing some of the issues of importance to all
Kiwis.
First of all, can I just say that one o f the things that is important is in regard to the
timing—and I know that there were comments made by New Zealand First, by Clayton
Mitchell. I think that was a good point, because timing is something that is important.
We know that other countries responded differently when it came to the issues of 9/11.
New Zealand is in a unique situation because, in a sense, it did respond —it did reduce
the number—and there are a couple of reasons for that. Part of it was to ensure that the
technology was available in o rder to detect any sort of fraudulent behaviour that may
have been happening. So that is what you would call the key issue that came to us.
When we talk about timing, as of now, returning back to the House, there are a
couple of things. There were two revi ews that were undertaken. One of those reviews
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4585
was in regard to the cost. Many people sort of thought: “Well, this is just a typical
Government situation where we go from 10 years to 5 years, where we put the cost up
to over $200 and it is generating revenue for the Government.” Can I just put on record,
before the House, that the Government does not actually gain any fees from the cost of
passports. It is done on a cost -recovery basis, so it is very minimal and is, actually, in
regard to the administration  costs for passports. So I just want to stake that out there.
This is not a Government money-generating exercise.
The second thing is just in regard to technology. We know that that is important as
we enter in and out of borders. New Zealand, in particular, has SmartGate, and we often
use that. I use it quite often now. It is a lot easier to be able to enter in and out using
SmartGate. Why? Because we now have the technology that is important and that
allows us to travel in and out quite easily and accessibly. In saying that, over 77 percent
of New Zealanders actually have a passport. The interesting thing about technology is
that over 40 percent of those who make renewals actually make them online. And so we
think that the investment in regard to technology is also really important.
I want to commend this bill to the select committee, and the work that it has to take. I
think it is important. It will be interesting to see the submissions that come out and
whether there are any changes. We think that this is a good bill, obviously. It is going to
a select committee that actually has a neutral perspective, in regard to its numbers,
because it is believed that, actually, this is something that is agreed on  commonly, right
across the House. I commend this  bill to the House and look forward to its return.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It is just as well that you called me, Mr
Deputy Speaker, because I was the only person taking the call. That is a big relief to me.
It is a real pleasure to participate in this debate on the Passports Amendment Bill (No
2). I want, first of all, to commend the Minister responsible for the bill, the Hon Peter
Dunne, and thank him for responding  to the recommendation of our Government
Administration Committee, which considered a petition on this very issue. It was a
really interesting consideration of a petition: learning about the background to the move
from the previous 10 year to 5- year passports, what other countries internationally had
done, and, of course, how technology has moved on. It was a mature debate at our
committee, and I know that the current membership will welcome this bill to be
considered by new members of the select committee.
I want to recommend a more mature approach to the consideration of policy issues,
particularly to the sole member from the ACT Party, David Seymour. I think he has got
a contribution to make to this House. I probably will not ever agree with him —I hope
not; it is unlikely—but I still think that in a democracy, in a valuable democracy such as
this Parliament, we should have different views heard. But I think it would be a good
thing for him to consider contributing to a debate from a less ideological and l ess
entrenched position. We all agree on this bill. It would be good to say that things have
moved on, we have changed our minds, instead of trying to throw grenades at a
Government that changed the law probably around the year he was born. It was not that
long ago; he is a young man. But I would recommend that.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Hey, look. You don’t talk about my age; I won’t talk about yours.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: And if the member does not want to take my advice on his
contribution in a better form, let me just say two words to him about this issue: David
Garrett. I would not go there, if I were you. I bet that party wished it had never, ever
gone near that person. But the issues of identification, the issues of fraud, the issues of
misrepresentation, the potential threat to our security —all bring David Garrett to mind,
actually—were the very reason that, at the time, officials recommended, and the
4586 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015
Government that I was proud to be part of accepted, the proposal that we move from 10
year to 5-year passports.
Since that time, my colleagues the Hon Trevor Mallard —a fine chair of the
Committee, on occasions —and the Hon Phil Goff have both campaigned really hard
within our party and outside it, actually, for the return of a 10- year passport. They were
both heavily involved in the discussion at the time when we moved from 10 years to 5
years, and understood the increased threat and risk and our lack of confidence in the
security of our systems at the time. They said things had moved on. The y persuaded
Labour of that. It was our policy at the last election to return to 10- year passports. They
argued it strongly when the petition came to our select committee. I think it was a
member of Mr Seymour’s party, actually, who brought that —you would know all the
members of your own party by name, I presume —Kyle Lockwood, and he was very
adequately supported by Jordan Williams from the taxpayers’ something -or-other
union. He is certainly an ACT member. But they actually did a very good presentation
on this issue to our committee.
So through all those pre -discussions, as I say, we have learnt a lot about the
changes—

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Actually, misleading the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: About what? I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am not
sure who said it, but a young man made a comment that I take offence at, and I require
him to withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: If the man could self-identify.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: I believe that the member is referring to me. I have been asked to
withdraw and apologise. I will not. The member said that a person is a member—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Be seated. The point is that the
member the Hon Ruth Dyson has taken offence at something the member has said. I did
not hear it myself. If she has taken offence, the member should withdraw and apologise.
Actually, I will just ask the Hon Ruth Dyson as to what it was that she took offence at.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: With respect, that would be repeating something that I say is
unparliamentary. I am happy to come and tell you, but I do not think it is helpful for the
order of the House to do that. But I give you my assurance that it was something that I
genuinely take offence at, and I am a fairly robust debater.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you. In that case, the member will stand,
withdraw, and apologise without comment.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker. So, back to the—

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The member has been stating
that certain individuals are a member of a political party I happen to lead, and that is
untrue.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: That is a matter of debate, and we will carry on.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Thank you for the clarification on what was not a point of
order. I want to absolutely apologise to Jordan Williams for saying that he was a
member of the ACT Party. I can understand why Mr Williams would be offended at
that. I thought he was; I apologise. I will never make that sort of assertion again.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Maybe we should come back to the bill.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: OK. It has been a bit of a tradition in the House over the last
few months to end the week on a bill on which there is agreement, and I am pretty sure
that there is unanimous agreement on this bill. I think it is a very good way for us to end
the week’s session.
I want to make a couple of comments on the specifics of the bill. It is interesting that
technology does not seem to allow us to replace photos of children. So children are still
18 Jun 2015 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 4587
going to have 5-year passports because their looks change more freq uently than adults’.
I would have thought that there may be enhanced technology to enable a photo to be
updated as a child ages rather than the entire passport having to be renewed. There has
been considerable debate about the cost of the passport. Origina lly, we were told that it
was going from 5 to 10 years and the cost would double. There was a bit of a shocked
reaction to that. It certainly does not take double the administration or double the
paperwork—literal paperwork in a passport —to extend it from 5 to 10 years, so I think
the Minister should be commended for his intervention then, and it seems to have got
back to a more reasonable rate.
There are some other specific areas in the bill that I think will warrant quite close
attention from the select committee. We want to get this right. We want to make sure
that the original reasons that we changed from 10 years to 5 years, and that was, as I
say, our lack of confidence in the robustness of our system, so that we could have
confidence that it was not being used for fraud and that it was not being used as a way
of having people enter our country when we did not want them to or that they were able
to change identity or misuse passports in any fraudulent way —so those issues, I think,
we will want to re-examine at the select committee, and we have had a good advance on
that through our petition deliberation.
Then there are other “let’s look to the future while we have this opportunity” chances
that this legislation will provide us with. For example, do we have to continue to do so
much of the work on paper? Can we do more online? What is the current situation in
regard to the security? I have been very impressed with the way the Department of
Internal Affairs has updated access to online renewal of passport s. Is that going to still
be maintained under the 10- year issue and will it give us the integrity without having
individual verification?
So, just in conclusion, I think this is a great note on which to end the week with
Parliament agreeing that this is a  good bill worthy of progress. The select committee
that I am privileged to chair will welcome it. I hope that we give it the level of scrutiny
that it deserves and I look forward to its further progress through the House.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: It is a privilege to speak on the
Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) in its first reading. Like the previous Government
member, Mr Ngaro, I do not sit on the Government Administ ration Committee, but it is
nevertheless a bill that will have an impact on many of my constituents. I was just
looking over the recent tourism numbers of those who travelled— and Mr McKelvie
touched on this —and in the last year there were 2.31 million New Zealand residents
who travelled overseas, which reached the highest record in our history and sees a 4
percent increase in international trips by New Zealand residents in the last year.
Interestingly, around half of those trips were to Australia, with the next most -visited
countries, in order, being the US, Fiji, the UK, China, and the Cook Islands. So that is a
fascinating fact for the day there.
I just want to touch on a point that Mr Clayton Mitchell made in his insightful
contribution around some of th e considerations that he would like to have seen put into
this bill. Particularly, there were a couple of suggestions around the number of pages in
passports potentially reducing, which somehow could reduce the administration costs
included there. Changing  the materials that passports are made of, also the colour
combinations used on passports, as well as the watermark solutions that could
potentially be on the pages would also potentially reduce the cost of passports. If you
combined simpler watermark solutions on the passport pages with reducing the number
of pages, it probably would save you one or two dollars. So there were very interesting
points made by New Zealand First.
4588 Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) 18 Jun 2015
Just getting back to the main provisions of the bill, we see that it will increa se the
validity of passports from 5 years to 10 years for citizens aged 16 and older. The
reasons behind children not being included in that have been well canvassed, and the
point was made by Ms Dyson just before around potentially some technology solutions
to include updated photos of children in passports. I think, yes, she is right that
technology has progressed, but one thing that has not progressed is magicianry. The
ability to take a blink and slip a photo in and out of a passport —I do not think we have
quite reached those technology levels yet. None the less, I would just like to reiterate
my support for this bill, and I look forward to seeing it proceed through the rest of the
parliamentary process. Thank you.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Government Administration Committee.

items.speaker: Minister of Internal Affairs
items.text: I move, T hat the Passports Amendment Bill (No 2) be
reported to the House by 30 October 2015.
Motion agreed to.
SOCIAL ASSISTANCE (PORTABILITY TO COOK ISLANDS, NIUE, AND
TOKELAU) BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I move, That the Social
Assistance (Portability to Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill be now read a third
time. This bill will provide greater pension flexibility for people who wish to live in the
Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. This Government wants to recognise  the great
contribution that people from those islands have made to New Zealand. We also want to
make sure that those countries and territories that have close constitutional ties with
New Zealand are recognised and that their ongoing economic and social viability is
supported. Current pension portability arrangements allow people to take their New
Zealand superannuation to 22 Pacific countries and territories, including the Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. The provision that makes this possible is called t he Special
Portability Arrangement.
Under this arrangement, New Zealand superannuation is paid at a minimum of 50
percent after 10 years’ residence in New Zealand, rising to 100 percent after 20 years’
residence. There are also general portability provisions, which cover people going to all
other countries with which New Zealand does not have a social security agreement. The
payment formula for the Special Portability Arrangement is more generous than the
payment formula for the general portability provisions. This is because the Special
Portability Arrangement is designed to recognise that contribution that Pacific peoples
have made to New Zealand and the inability of Pacific countries and territories to fulfil
the reciprocal obligations necessary to conclude social security agreements with N ew
Zealand.
Despite the relative generosity of the Special Portability Arrangement, an issue for
people who wish to retire in the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau is that under the
arrangement they must be resident and present in New Zealand on the date th ey apply
for New Zealand superannuation. Consequently, people who wish to receive New
Zealand superannuation in those islands are not able to leave New Zealand until they are
65, which is the age of eligibility for New Zealand superannuation. Should they c hoose
to return permanently to the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau prior to age 65, they lose
their ability to apply for New Zealand superannuation. This bill will remedy that
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4589
situation by eliminating the resident and present in New Zealand requirement for  the
Special Portability Arrangement in respect of the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. The
bill will allow people to move to those islands after reaching the age of 55 and apply for
the New Zealand superannuation or veterans pension from these Pacific Islands at age
65. People still need to live in New Zealand until they are 55 because in order to be
eligible for New Zealand superannuation or a veterans pension, a person must have
lived in New Zealand for 10 years since the age of 20, 5 of which must be af ter the age
of 50. The residence rule applies to all applicants for New Zealand superannuation.
There has been a lot of debate in the House on this point. I want to make it clear that
all New Zealanders must meet the 5 over 50 rule regardless of who they are and where
they live. New Zealand superannuation is based on principles of fair and equitable
treatment, and it would not be fair and equitable to allow a small group of New
Zealanders to avoid a rule simply because of where they choose to live, when every
other New Zealander must fulfil that rule. Members have also said that it is unfair that
migrants can come to New Zealand and qualify for full New Zealand superannuation
after 10 years’ residence in New Zealand, whereas people who want to live in and
receive their pension in the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau must have had 20 years’
residence in New Zealand to get the full payment available. This bill reflects the
universal nature of New Zealand superannuation. All applicants living in New Zealand
will receive full superannuation after 10 years’ residence. This Government believes
that all New Zealanders, regardless of where they were born, deserve to be treated
equally.
Where applicants want to receive their New Zealand pension in another country,
though, we apply a different set of residency requirements. This can vary between
countries, depending on the details of the relevant legislative provisions or social
security agreement. As I have already said, people who live in the Pacific, including the
Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau, have a relatively generous payment formula compared
with people who take New Zealand superannuation anywhere else in the world. If a
person moved to another country, they would need to have lived in New Zealand for
between 40  and 45 years to be eligible for full New Zealand superannuation. To be
clear, those who live in New Zealand qualify for full New Zealand superannuation after
10 years’ residence, including 5 years after the age of 50. Those who choose to live in
the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau qualify for 50 percent of New Zealand
superannuation after 10 years’ residence and full superannuation after 20 years’
residence. They must be resident in New Zealand for 5 years after the age of 50. Those
who choose to live in another country subject to portability agreements would generally
need to have lived in New Zealand for 45 years to be eligible for full superannuation.
However, there can be some difference between agreements.
Some members have also said that the bill disc riminates against people from the
Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. There is no inequality here. People from those i slands
who remain in New Zealand are subject to exactly the same rules as all other New
Zealanders. They will receive full New Zealand superannuation after 10 years’
residence. All people who wish to take New Zealand superannuation to the Cook
Islands, Niue, or Tokelau are subject to the rules in the special portability provisions,
regardless of whether they were born in New Zealand, the Islands, or another part of the
world. The change in this bill is restricted to the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau
because it is about recognising New Zealand’s close constitutional relationships with
these Pacific Islands, which enjoy shared citizenship with N ew Zealand and unique
legal arrangements. Tokelau is a non -selfgoverning territory of New Zealand. Both the
Cook Islands and Niue have adopted constitutions enabling self -government in free
4590 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
association with New Zealand. Free association is a status distinc t from that of full
independence in that it allows for the Cook Islands and Niue to maintain New Zealand
citizenship while administering their own affairs.
As I mentioned earlier, this bill is also about ensuring the economic and social
viability of the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. Depopulation and its related social and
economic consequences is a longstanding issue for those islands. The current “resident
and present in New Zealand” requirement has been described as a disincentive for Cook
Islanders, Niueans, and Tokelauans who are established in New Zealand to return home
before the age of 65. Removing this disincentive would potentially help boost economic
development and human resource capability in these islands through an increased return
of experienced people who are able to effectively apply skills acquired in New Zealand
in their home communities. People returning at age 55 would have the capacity to
contribute to the workforce 10 years in advance of the age of qualification for New
Zealand superannuation. As pension payments are paid in gross, it is expected that more
income and value-added tax will be paid by returning migrants to contribute to the local
economy.
I want to reiterate that this Government wants to make sure that those countries and
territories that have close constitutional ties with New Zealand are recognised and that
their ongoing economic and social viability is supported. This Government also wants
to ensure that superannuitants have options as to where they choose to live. B y allowing
people to apply for New Zealand superannuation and the veterans pension while
resident in the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau, this bill will achieve both of these
things. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: Kia orana, fakalofa lahi atu, and
taloha ni. It is a privilege to speak on the third reading of this bill. I want to
acknowledge all of our Cook Island, Niue, and Tokelau -  New Zealand residents living
in New Zealand, and all of our Tokelau, Cook Island, and Niue people living in the
Realm of New Zealand countries.
We come here today all in support of this bill, with one minor —or not so minor —
point that we disagree with. Listening to the Minister for Social Development, there was
much of what she said that I agreed with; some of what she said I thought: “Hang on a
second, that’s not actually correct, Minister.” One of the points she raised was that all
New Zealanders must meet the 5 years after 5 0 rule in terms of 5 years having been
spent in New Zealand over the age of 50, regardless of where they live, to be able to
access their superannuation.
We know —and this has put forward through a Supplementary Order Paper —that,
actually, there are countr ies where we have a reciprocal pension agreement. They are
countries like Australia, the UK, and the Netherlands, where, actually, they can access
their pension there without having to spend 5 years in New Zealand between the ages of
50 and 65. What we have been asking for, alongside New Zealand First, is that that
same exemption be given to these three countries, which have a special constitutional
relationship with New Zealand. Actually, if any citizens were going to be exempt from
that 5-year rule, it sh ould be the three countries that are actually part of the Realm of
New Zealand. So to hear the Minister go on and say that there is no justification or
rationale for an exemption, well, actually, I think that that is incorrect, and the
submissions that we received from people like the Prime Minister of the Cook Islands
and the Premier of Niue actually should have been enough to persuade the National
Government and to convince it that an exemption was warranted in this particular case.
Many of us of Pacific descent in this House have an understanding of the importance
of returning to the Pacific country that we came from. I myself have a father who was
born and raised in Samoa and who has now, in his later years, gone back to Samoa to
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4591
invest in the land, to renew the plantation, and to get people working on that plantation.
It has made a huge difference to our family over there in terms of —here is this
plantation that was not touched for almost 30 years, and now there is this whole family
