that has found this renewed interest in the land that had kind of been left to itself for just
a long period of time.
Niue, the Cook Islands, and Tokelau have the same possibilities, and we have an
opportunity here to support these citizens to return to those countries, to i nvest in their
own countries, and to contribute to their economic development. For the Minister to say
that that investment can start at age 55, or that that investment can start in those years
but they must still spend 5 years here between the ages of 50 and 65, well, actually, that
is not good enough.
One of the biggest issues that we have been told about by these countries is that we
have depleted them of their major resource —their major resource —that being their
people. We look at places at Niue, which now has a population of something like 1,200
people. How can it develop its economy with 1,200 people when we have 24,000 of its
people in this country? Those are 24,000 people who have contributed to this country,
not only to our workforce, to our sports  fields, to our academic credentials but also —
and I think this is really important to point out —serving under the New Zealand flag
alongside our military at war. Yet we have a Minister and a National Government who
cannot give that one exemption that was a sked for, that being to exempt them from the
5-year rule between the ages of 50 and 65.
If we had had agreement on that one small point, I think we would all be celebrating
in the House today. We would have consensus here, and, actually, we would be happy
with each other. But when we walk out the door today and we go and talk to our Niue,
Tokelau, and Cook Island communities, yes, we can say that we have made some
arrangement so that the portability has increased for them, so that they can go back
earlier and they can contribute, but not to the extent that we think we should have.
Let me just say that members on that side of the House need to know that when we
walk out this door we will be saying to our Cook Island, Niue, and Tokelau
communities that, yes,  there was consensus overall for the bill, but we were
disappointed, Labour was disappointed, that National could not understand the rationale
or see the justification for exempting our three Realm countries from that one rule that
would allow them to spend 15 of their years between the ages of 50 and 65 back in their
homelands. Exempting them from that one rule would have allowed them 5 additional
years between those age groups to contribute to the economic development of their own
countries. National woul d not agree that the historical and constitutional ties we have
with those three countries were enough to actually warrant an exemption. So we will be
going out there and voicing that to our communities.
Actually, already I did see that my colleague Poto Williams did put something up on
social media and the reaction she got from the Cook Island community about the fact
that the one Cook Island MP in the National Party could not convince his National Party
colleagues to support that one exemption was actual ly—let us just say they were
outraged that had happened. You know, we know that regardless of whatever ethnicity
we are, there are ideologies, philosophies, and ways of thinking in different political
parties, and this is one of those examples where, actua lly, the rest of our community
gets to see that that exists regardless of ethnicity, that there is a philosophy and ideology
that comes with an individual, depending on which political party they are in. That has
proven itself today and with this whole discussion around the bill.
I am not sure, actually, whether I have more to contribute to this discussion. The
point I wanted to make today was that, actually, yes, we are happy to support this bill.
We are disappointed in the National Government, that it did not understand the rationale
4592 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
for exempting Niue, Tokelau, and the Cook Islands from the 5- year rule. We will be
letting our communities know that that was the case, but in the very least this is a step
forward. It is a step towards recognising the special relationship we have with the three
Realm countries. I will end on a positive note and say that, at the very least, that is a
good thing. Thank you.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: It is nice to finish on a positive note
there. It is a pleasure to speak on the Social Assistance (Portability to Cook Islands,
Niue, and Tokelau) Bill. I think there is general agreement across the House that this is
a good bill. With the Realm countries electing to have self -governance and free
association, it is a wonderful thing to be able to align them with the same rights to be
able to retire and take your superannuation with you to the Islands.
Although there has been a lot of talk about those rules —I think I will touch on that a
bit further on— I first want to talk a little bit about the submissions that were given to
the Social Services Committee. Generally they were mostly, all except for one, focused
on the 5 years over 50 provision in the bill, and two of them, in fact, suggested that the
5 years over 50 should be 5 years over 40, giving people a bit longer in the Islands. The
rationale, of course, is that those people would be able to contribute more to the
economy of those islands and contribute to the communities as well. Although I suggest
that that is a very good idea in spirit, they will actually get that at age 55 anyway.
Although we are aligning this with what every New Zealander has to do to qualify
for superannuation, I think I would just like  to point out that in those countries we have
agreements with, like Australia and the UK, as was pointed out before, what is different
about that situation is that there is a provision known as totalisation. That provision
allows for reciprocal payments of  superannuation within those nations. That does not
apply in the Islands, because they are not able to pay their superannuation at the same
rate.
So in theory it sounds good to hand out a little bit more money, and I know the
rationale of some members of the Opposition in the Committee debate was that it is not
that much money, so why do we not just pay it. Well, my running total so far, at the
moment, when adding all of these up in these various bills through the House, is half a
billion dollars. So these  little bits of money add up to quite a lot of money and, being
legislators, we have to make hard decisions. We take taxes off New Zealand citizens
and distribute them to provide the services that the Government provides, and
superannuation is one of those . In this bill we must be responsible with that money, as
we are with every other bill we debate in this House.
On the whole I think we can be very proud of this bill. I think the people of the Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau can all be very, very pleased with this. I would also like to
take note that my colleague Alfred Ngaro reminds us that the triple star that is referred
to in our national anthem refers to these nations. I think that probably should be spoken
about at every opportunity, because most pe ople do not realise that that is what it refers
to. I think it is a great thing. In summary, I think this is a great bill and I have a lot of
pleasure in commending it to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Kia orana, Mr Speaker. In
February I had the pleasure of travelling to Rarotonga to attend a United Nations
development partners meeting. They had an award ceremony on one of the nights I was
there, and during the award ceremony they made an award to my uncle, Mr Tekake
Williams. Tekake Williams is a pioneer of the black pearl industry. Many of the people
from this House who have travelled to the Cook Islands know that the black pearl is one
of the major components of the economy in the Cooks. My father, Nahora Williams,
used to travel back to the Cooks to help his younger brother work in the pearl farm in
the early days. When my father retired he would travel every year to the Cooks for a
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4593
couple of months —he would winter up there —and he would be very pleased to know
that we are putting this bill through the House and that it will be passed tonight.
Portability was important to him. He did not have the opportunity to access the
portability that is now being  afforded, so in that regard today is a very important day
because the bill will be passed and afford to many people the opportunity that my father
did not have. My father, I should also say, used to travel to the Cooks and leave mother
behind, but that is a whole other issue.
Portability is important because, as my colleague Carmel Sepuloni said, one of the
unintended consequences of being part of the countries of the Realm of New Zealand
and travelling on a New Zealand passport is the depopulation of the  home islands. We
are able to travel freely as people of the Realm to New Zealand and we have done so,
not only to New Zealand but also to Australia. So this portability bill is an attempt, I
guess, to support the travel home, the return home, of people in order that they
contribute to the economy of their home islands.
But what is difficult about it—and we have traversed this well and truly across the
House during the passage of this bill —has been the difficulty around the residency
clause that mentions “ after the age of 50”. Twelve of the 13 submitters were very clear
that they felt that clause was a huge barrier to the opportunity to make a significant
difference to the economy of the Cooks and to the population of the Cooks —and I
speak of the example of  the Cooks because I have personal knowledge of this. The
opportunity that my father, for example, may have had to go back and actually start a
pearl farm of his own, had he been able to do so, cannot be afforded to him, and there
are many people who are currently in the countries of the Realm who will have to return
to do that 5 year residency. It is blatantly unfair when we have portability arrangements
with other countries that do not have that as a provision. It is unfair.
We had the benefit of having the Hon Henry Puna, the Hon Nandi Glassie, and
Premier Talagi from Niue here to present, and the very fact that we had two heads of
State and a Government Minister from overseas countries come and present to our
select committee should have been recognised  for the value that it brought. They were
coming to plead their case, and that, unfortunately, fell on a couple of deaf ears. There
was also the hard work by the Matua group, and I have to acknowledge the group in
Christchurch led by Mama Tufunga and Papa John Pitomaki, who were very
impassioned in their submission and quoted the sacrifice they felt they and their families
who had come before them had given to this country. I have already in this House
talked about the 500 soldiers from the Cook Islands who fought for New Zealand under
the New Zealand flag during World War I. What has that afforded to us? In this bill it is
demonstrated that that sacrifice has been for nothing. I also want to commend the
submission made by the Christian Church in Christchurc h by Mrs Teremoana McNabb.
She too spoke quite passionately about the residency requirement post age 50 and how
unequal that made her feel as a Cook Islander living in New Zealand.
But there was hope. There was hope in the form of the Supplementary Order Paper
that was put forward by New Zealand First. It was supported by us. It was a good
Supplementary Order Paper and it was an attempt to redress an inequality that exists
within this bill. After the Committee stage, as my colleague Carmel Sepuloni has said, I
was canvassed quite heavily by members of the Cook Islands community to ask: what
now? What now? What can we do now? Unfortunately, for this bill, that is it. We will
not actually be able to demonstrate our commitment to our Cook Islands, Niue, and
Tokelau communities as we would have hoped. We will not be able to say that, yes,
your sacrifice, your hard work, and the lives of your ancestors do mean something to
New Zealand, and, yes, we will bring you in line with portability arrangements with
4594 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
other countries that do not have the special arrangements. But in this case we cannot say
that.
I also have to acknowledge the RSA submitter who made a very clear case that when
you receive a war pension, that  is not the same as superannuation. He wanted it noted
on the record that someone who puts their life at risk in service of this country should be
recognised differently to someone who receives a pension because they have been a
taxpayer and it is the age of eligibility that triggers that. I want to acknowledge that
RSA submitter and say yes, I agree that someone who does put their life on the line for
their country should be treated in a different way and acknowledged in a different way.
Superannuation and war pensions should be treated separately, so I acknowledge the
work that you have done.
So I say to all of those people —and there will be one or two who are watching the
third reading of this —that we did try. We tried really hard. We did our best, but i t has
not come to fruition as you would have hoped. But we all know that there is one person
whom we can point to on the other side of the House who could have stood up for you
but chose not to—someone who could have petitioned his colleagues and talked about
his own family experience but chose not to. I am not going to belabour the rest of this
bill. I am pleased about the provisions that we are passing in this bill, and it will make it
possible for some people to have the opportunities that they may not have had prior. But
at the end of the day it does not do what was promised by Mr McCully all those years
ago, and for that I am very disappointed. Kia orana. Meitaki maata.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: After that speech by Poto Williams I
struggled to get to my feet —what a sombre affair. It just drained the energy out of me.
What a great day for the Cook Islands, what a great day for Niue, what a great day for
Tokelau, and what a great day for all New Zealanders, who now will not need to be
resident and present in New Zealand to receive their superannuation. This is just typical
petty oppositional politics —everything we do, they will say it is not good enough.
Imagine if we gave every vu lnerable family in New Zealand $25 a week. They would
still say that was not enough —hold on, we did do that, and they still said that was not
enough. What a great day for the Cook Islands, for Tokelau, and for Niue. What a great
day for all New Zealanders, who will be able to retire at the age of 65 and not have to be
resident and present in New Zealand.
Can I say kia orana to the Cook Islands, taloha ni to Tokelau, and fakalofa lahi atu to
Niue. I do not have any ancestral connections to these i slands but, as I disclosed in my
second reading speech, it was in Rarotonga in the Cook Islands that I got down on my
knees on the beach and proposed to my wife. I could not think of a better environment
to start a beautiful relationship, and I could not think of a better environment to retire to.
This bill is being passed, so what a great day this is.
On Wednesday of this week I was at the Budget estimates hearing for Vote Social
Development. I think we need to remind ourselves where the funding comes from. Vote
Social Development is the biggest spender of this Budget at $25 billion —$25 billion.
The country trusts us with the management of this money. It was demonstrated very
clearly in September last year that they trust us, that they know we are responsible. That
is why they returned us to Government. In Vote Social Development the focus of the
Government’s work is to move people from dependence to independence. It was great
to see the programmes like the Community Investment Strategy, which will deliver this.
Can I pay homage not only to the Minister for Social Development, Anne Tolley, for
this bill but also to the chair of the Social Services Committee, Alfred Ngaro. Like
many people in this Chamber, we wear many hats. At times we look at things through a
personal lens, and at other times we look at things through a professional lens. It is very
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4595
disappointing that people on the other side of the House have blurred those lenses from
personal to professional and forgotten the very important roles that we play.
It is somewhat interesting that the members opposite have selective memory about
the submissions. The submissions process was, yes, overly favourable. I remember the
Concerned Community Collective. It was great to see about 30 people get together from
ages 25 to 75. It shows the key interest of this bill, because they all can see the benefit,
but the Opposition clearly forgets.
There were concerns around this bill around people moving back to the Islands and
the pressure that would put on housing, on social s ervices, and on health. That is why it
is good to structure the process as we have done, to take the steps we have done to see
how this will play out. Of course, these islands need repopulation, and it is great that we
will be able to promote economic deve lopment in these i slands. Not only is it about
people returning home to spend their hard -earned superannuation to support the local
businesses in Tokelau, Niue, and the Cook Islands but it is about the tourism as well —
the pensioner tourism. They will be able to go over and spend money in these islands.
This bill amends the payments for New Zealand superannuation. Currently, people
have to reside and be present in New Zealand at 65. This change will allow applicants
who are 65 to apply from these countries. It was great to hear the thinking that has
already happened about the roll -out and the phasing -in of the IT support that will be
needed to facilitate these payments. It shows that this Government —trustworthy and
responsible—has clearly thought through the pragmatic implementation of this bill.
We must remind ourselves that this bill is not only for people from Niue, Tokelau,
and the Cook Islands. This bill is for all New Zealanders. They will be able to go and
retire in these countries and enjoy a blessed  retirement. Thank you. I support this bill to
the House.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I rise to take the first call for the Greens on the third
reading of the Social Assistance (Portability to Cook Islands, N iue, and Tokelau) Bill .
We are pleased to be supporting this bill in its final reading and we will, of course, be
voting for it. This bill recognises, and should recognise, the special relationship that
New Zealand has with the countries of the Realm of New Zealand: the Cook Islands,
Niue, and Tokelau. It is a special relationship that has lasted a long time.
This bill changes what has been seen to be an inequity. I have to say that the
evidence we heard during the Social Services Committee hearings suggested that this
bill has been a long time coming, and, certainly, that is the view of my colleagues over
here who were also on the select committee at the time. It was a special privilege to
have the premier leaders of our Realm countries come and present their oral
submissions to the select committee. It is not something that happens very often, but I
would reiterate that it was an absolute signal from these countries that a change to
superannuation and the veterans pension portability is absolutely required for the
citizens of the Realm who want to go back and spend their final years in those Island
nations.
What the bill does is enable citizens of the Realm from those island nations who have
lived in New Zealand for more than 10 years after the age of 20 to return to their home
country while remaining eligible for New Zealand superannuation, as long as they have
lived in New Zealand for 5 years after the age of 50. This provision was quite
controversial, and I want to acknowledge and thank the members on this side of the
House f rom both New Zealand First and Labour who put up Supplementary Order
Papers in an attempt to amend that provision in the bill, because we do still see that as
an inequity. What the bill does is allow, after the age of 55, citizens from Niue, Tokelau,
and Cook Islands  to return to their home islands and to apply for and receive New
Zealand superannuation and the veterans pension if they are eligible for it. The previous
4596 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
situation was that they had to be present and resident in New Zealand in order to access
that superannuation.
When the Act actually comes into being it will not actually affect a huge amount of
people right away. Roughly about 250 only will be triggered into being able to access
superannuation and the veterans pension. However, it does give an opportunity for those
many people from the three Realm countries living in New Zealand to be able to access
it in the future, which we do see as fairer.
Currently, according to Statistics New Zealand, there are 62,000 people from the
Cook Islands, 23,000 Niueans, and 7,176 people from Tokelau living here, and those
are far greater numbers than the populations living on those i slands themselves. It has
been an ongoing issue that the local economies have been depleted of their greatest
resource, which, I agree with my colleague Poto Williams, is their people. So we have a
larger number of people living in New Zealand, then, than are living in the Realm
islands. But their connections are strong and their ancestral ties bind them to those
countries, and it is  fair and reasonable that they return in their final years, if they want
to, to take up their lives back in their home country. The depopulation issue has been a
real problem, and we did hear that from the leaders of those countries when they
submitted, but we did also hear that there was some potential for this change in this bill
to enable people to return to their country at the age of 55, when they may—they may—
be young enough to be able to contribute further to the economies in their home
countries. But we are not sure about that; that was one of the reasons why we were quite
keen to remove the 5 years after 50 rule.
We are happy to be supporting this bill and to know that it is supported unanimously
across the House. It is very rare that that happens and it is an unusual experience, I have
to say, but for the people of the Realm and from the Realm countries I think it is
something we should be doing, to ensure that they get the best deal that we can possibly
give them. Again, I restate that I am disapp ointed that the National Party did not listen
to the submitters that we heard, including those from those nations’ leaders, asking for
more flexibility, because they have been waiting and they have been negotiating with
Murray McCully and others in the Nat ional Government for a very long time. So
although this bill does not go as far as we would like it to go, it is a step forward and we
will be supporting it.

items.speaker: DARROCH BALL
items.text: New Zealand First has made it quite clear from the
start where we stand on this bill. We do agree with the changes that are being made, but
it is not good enough. We did put in Supplementary Order Paper 71 and requested
support from the Government; in particular, from one member of the Government, at
least, who knows that he should have voted for that Supplementary Order Paper. We
have had support and the same way of thinking from all the Opposition parties in regard
to the Supplementary Order Paper, and that Supplementary Order Paper was specifically
in regard to the 5 years over 50 rule.
I would just like to talk about something that Matt Doocey said in his speech
previously, and that was that this was nothing but petty Opposition politics —
disagreeing with things or think ing that the changes are never good enough. Well, I
would like him to have a look at the submissions, and who submitted and what they
submitted on. There were 13 submissions and 12 of them were in regard to the 5 years
over 50 part of the amendment. I woul d like him to contact the Prime Minister of the
Cook Islands and tell him that this is nothing but petty politics, because it is not. It
shows the importance, the outright importance, of that specific clause to the people of
those three Realm countries. In fact, we had a unique situation where the Prime Minister
of the Cook Islands and the Premier of Niue, I believe it was, came over personally and
gave an oral submission. That is the importance that they placed on that clause. In fact,
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4597
what the Government of the Cook Islands submitted was that the Cook Islands did
support the bill but recommended further consideration, given the 5 years over 50 rule.
Not only that, the submitters actually made a good point where they pointed out that the
regulatory impact s tatement did not actually mention the financial burden placed on
New Zealand by applicants who may claim welfare payments returning to satisfy the 5 -
year residence requirement. So from the get -go in the process —and I know that there
has actually been a lon g time going through the process of this bill—it seemed to me,
when I was going through it in the select committee and through these different stages,
that there was not actually a lot of thought put into the bill itself. The reason why I say
that is—

items.speaker: Jono Naylor
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: DARROCH BALL
items.text: Well, Mr Naylor might disagree with that, but I ask him to look
at all of the submissions and see what the opposition to that clause is and who is saying
it. It is not just the Opposition parties; it is the people who are being affected by that
clause specifically—and that is the importance of that clause.
What I would also like to go on to are the purpose and intent. The reason why I say
there was not much thought put into the bill is because the pur pose and the intent of the
bill are actually good ones. They are to recognise the very special relationship that New
Zealand as a country has with those three Island nations. They come under the Realm of
New Zealand, and the Cook Islands, as Mr Ngaro would know, even uses the New
Zealand dollar. So not only have we got ancestral connections with those i slands but we
have the largest population centre —being Auckland —of the Pacific Islands, and, in
particular, of those three. We have economic ties. They come under our protectorate. So
the bill misses out on that very important provision on the 5 years over 50, which those
islands have been asking for, for a very, very long time. I think that the Government
assumed that this would be a bill that would pass through the House quite easily and
uncontested. But that was not the case. New Zealand First put through a minority report
stating those different points.
But I would just like to touch on the extra costs that the departmental report from the
Ministry of Soci al Development said that it would actually cost. We are not talking
about a huge number of people this would affect, but it would make such a big impact
in their lives—and, more important, their families’ lives. If we are talking just about the
administrative implications for the ministry, in 2020, in 5 years’ time, we are talking
about only $60,000 to $65,000 in administrative costs. That is the cost that the
Government is saying is one of the reasons why it will not change that clause. We are
talking about up to 100 additional applications for New Zealand superannuation in
subsequent years, and it costs the ministry only around a million dollars a year. If you
compare that with a waste of money like the flag referendum, which is costing $30
million, you can see where the Government puts its priority.
New Zealand First, like I said, is supporting this bill. We support the intent; we
support the purpose. We do not think it goes far enough and for very good reason. I
would like to join my Labour colleagues in saying to those people  out there whom this
does affect that we tried our hardest. We put in the Supplementary Order Paper. All it
would have taken was one member across in the Government benches to vote for the
Supplementary Order Paper, but he did not.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker, for the
opportunity to take this call to speak on the Social Assistance (Portability to Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill  in its third reading. This is a great bill for the Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau because this bill seeks to provide greater pension flexibility
for those people who wish to retire in these three Pacific nations —Cook Islands, Niue,
and Tokelau.
4598 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
This bil l, as acknowledged by the member who just spoke, Darroch Ball, is about
recognising our special constitutional ties with these three Pacific nations, which enjoy
shared New Zealand citizenship and unique legal arrangements. Under our current
portability arrangement eligible people are required to be residents and present here in
New Zealand at the time of applying for their superannuation at the age of 65. This bill
is to remove that requirement.
There is a residence condition, which is that to be eligible  for New Zealand
superannuation or the veterans pension people should have lived here for 10 years after
the age of 20, which includes 5 years after the age of 50. This means that people —those
who wish to—can actually retire in these three Island countries  at the age of 55. They
can go to these Island countries to retire at the age of 55 and when they turn 65 they can
apply for their New Zealand superannuation from any of these three Pacific nations.
The Social Services Committee received 13 submissions an d they were thoroughly
considered. Six were orally heard and I can say that most of those submissions were in
support of this bill. I want to acknowledge our chair, Alfred Ngaro, and I also want to
acknowledge our Minister, the Hon Anne Tolley, for the wor k that she has done on this
bill. I also want to acknowledge all submitters for the time they took to come and make
those submissions. We had thorough discussions on points that were raised.
One issue that came up and widely discussed was depopulation. This was actually
linked to the 5 years after 50 rule. I also note the Supplementary Order Paper 71 by
New Zealand First to make a change to exempt these three Pacific nations, the Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau, from this 5 years after 50 rule.
I was here in the Chamber when we were debating the Committee stage of this bill.
My observation was that I did not expect Labour to be fair. The New Zealand First
members were pleading to get support for this Supplementary Order Paper, but they
could not provide even a single reason why their Supplementary Order Paper should be
supported. The only reason that came from their side was that it is not that many people;
it is not about how many people. It is about fairness, and it is about having a balanced
approach. That was coming from the party that thinks it has some common sense. It
thinks it has some common sense, but there was no common sense in its Supplementary
Order Paper, to get support.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: No common sense.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: No common sense.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Common sense is decidedly uncommon.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: That is true. There was no common sense. There was
no fairness. There was no reason given as to why that rule should be amended. It was
very interesting for me to sit here and watch that.
But this National Government is committed to all. This National Government is
working for all. We are an efficient and fair Government. We are not unfair, like the m.
This bill going through does not mean that it will apply only to those people who
originally came from the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau. Once this bill goes through,
this provision will be available to all those eligible people, those who wish to reti re in
these three Pacific nations. It is the kind of flexibility that we want to provide to people.
It does not mean that all people, those who are from the Cook Islands, Niue, and
Tokelau, will take up this provision. So it is about providing greater flex ibility. We
know that there are around 650 people in the Pacific who are receiving New Zealand
superannuation, and out of those 650 people around 300 are in the Cook Islands. We
also know that with this legislation going through, there will be around 245 people who
will benefit, with an increase of 16 people per year.
The New Zealand Government is always committed to its relationship with the
Pacific nations. We have strong cultural, political, and economic ties with the Pacific
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4599
nations. With these three Pacific nations, the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau, we have
a very special relationship. We call it free association. As a result of this free association
the people from these three Pacific nations enjoy New Zealand superannuation and also
there is subst antial assistance from our Government to their Governments, so there is
this very close linkage. Employment opportunities here in New Zealand are better, so it
is natural that the people from these Pacific nations are attracted to New Zealand.
With these three Pacific nations there is even greater attraction because their people
have New Zealand citizenship and rights to residence. The issue of depopulation is a
real one. That is why this bill is really important. It is to help these three Pacific nations
with that issue. This bill will make people go to these Pacific nations, if they wish to, at
the age of 55, and at the age of 65 they can apply for their New Zealand superannuation
from any of these three Pacific nations.
This National Government recognis es that New Zealanders have worked hard and
they deserve to enjoy their retirement. We want them to have as many options as
possible. It is very hard to say what the cost of this to the Crown will be, but we know
that this move will definitely help these three Pacific nations —the Cook Islands, Niue,
and Tokelau. This bill is to help these three Pacific nations socially and economically,
and it will also reduce the impact of depopulation that they have in these three Pacific
nations.
This bill is about keeping it fair. Once the bill goes through, it will be applicable to
all eligible people—those who wish to retire in these three Pacific nations. This 5 years
after 50 rule applies to all, even to New Zealand - born people—those who have gone
overseas and com e back and want to spend their retirement here or those who want to
go to other countries and spend their retirement there. It is about fairness, and it is about
having a balanced approach. As I said, this National Government is about fairness. We
analyse everything from a fairness point of view. That is why we are not supporting the
exemption to the 5 years after 50 rule in Supplementary Order Paper 71.
This bill is a great bill to support these three Pacific nations. This bill is about
recognising our special relationship with these three Pacific nations. I am really
delighted to commend this bill to the House, and to support it. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call will be a split call.
Jan Logie—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I rise to take a short call on the third reading of the Social
Assistance (Portability to Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill. The Green Party is, of
course, supporting this bill. We are united with this side of the House in disappointment
that it does not go far enough. I will explain to members of the public what this bill is
about. It is about enabling people who live in the Realm of New Zealand—Niu e,
Tokelau, and the Cook Islands—to access superannuation or their veterans pension after
they have worked in New Zealand for 10 to 20 years, and to access it without having to
be in New Zealand on the age of retirement.
The bill still requires people to live in New Zealand for 5 years post the age of 50,
which is our contention with this bill. Partly, it is because this has been an issue that has
been raised with members in this House for decades. It has been a real concern for
people from these countries , who are part of our Realm. They are part of our family.
They are not another country per se. They are part of the Realm of New Zealand. They
have been saying that these rules have been creating an incentive for people to stay in
New Zealand when they would have otherwise returned to their country, to be able to
engage in meaningful work pre -retirement. When we look at the example of Niue,
which for me is the most striking, there are fewer than 1,600 people left on the island
and over 23,000 are here in Ne w Zealand. We can see the impact of this kind of
regulation on that country, and, by virtue of the impact on them, the impact on our
4600 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
overseas development and aid budget. So where there is a small cost here, there is also a
potential savings in overseas dev elopment and aid support from New Zealand. This is
about seeing this whole situation holistically and addressing it holistically, but also, to
me, it is fundamentally a matter of respect.
Two heads of State presented  before the select committee, which is a very rare
occurrence. They spoke directly to this House about what a difference it would make to
be able to pass this legislation and to remove that 5 years post 50 years of age
requirement. They said that it would absolutely assist their countries in re versing the
depopulation, building their economies, and sustaining their communities. I think it is
very sad that the Government has chosen to go only part -way in addressing those
concerns, and I think it is short -sighted. I do not think it makes sense, in terms of even
the medium-term economic interests of this country, let alone those Realm countries’
interests, for the Government to make this decision. I think it is very short -sighted and
poor thinking.
I do particularly want to acknowledge the Realm countries as part of our family, and
the contribution of the people who have left their countries to come to our country, right
here. They are people who have contributed massively to our economy, to our societies,
to our academic sphere, and to this Parliament, for goodness’ sake. They are people who
have died under the colours of this country in war. Where their needs are met only part -
way by this Government, I find it disrespectful and another example of unnecessary
meanness. Although we are happy to support this bill for the step that it does take, we
are disappointed that it could not go the whole way in honouring the contribution of all
those people. Kia ora.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Louisa Wall—5 minutes.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Tēnā koe, te Māngai o te Whare. Kia
orana. Fakalofa atu ki a mutolu osi. Malo ni. It is my pleasure to speak on this, the third
reading of the Social Assistance (Portability to Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill. I
would like to take this opportunity to pay my respects to the two heads of State —Cook
Islands Prime Minister Henry Puna and Premier Talagi from Niue —who came to our
country and, in a very rare occurrence, made a submission to the select committee.
From my perspective, I think the significance of that submission really needs to be
reflected in the final debate in the House, because what it speaks to, actually, is the
prioritisation, from their perspective, of this piece of legislation.
I just want to outline quickly the eligibility for New Zealand superannuation. For
people who are listening: you have to be 65 years of age, you have to be a citizen or
resident, you have to have lived here for 10 years since the age of 20, and you also have
to have lived here for 5 years since the age of 50. Generally, you have to be a resident in
New Zealand on the date of application. Those are the general rules, or criteria, around
New Zealand superannuation.
If you are from the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau, you are a citizen of this country
by virtue of having been born in one of those countries. They are Realm countries of
New Zealand, so they are incredibly special, and they have a special status in terms of
us here in Aotearoa. You have to have spent 20 years in New Zealand since the age of
20, and 5 years since the age of 50, but under this legislation—and this is where I want
to congratulate the Government —you can now apply from the Cook Islands, Niue, and
Tokelau for your pension. So, well done; congratulations. On behalf of the people of the
Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau, I would like to say thank you, because I think it is
significant. In fact, it is one of the two things that the P rime Minister of the Cook
Islands and the Premier of Niue came to submit about.
Half of what they asked for has been achieved. In terms of the differences, obviously,
being able to apply from those Realm countries is incredibly important. The other
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4601
difference that I want to highlight is that unlike general New Zealanders, who have to
have been here for 10 years since the age of 20, in fact, if you come from the Cook
Islands, Niue, or Tokelau, you actually have to have lived in New Zealand for 20 years.
And that was the main contention, particularly, of the submission by the Prime Minister
of the Cook Islands to the select committee. If you are a general New Zealander, it is 10
years; if you are from the Cook Islands, it is 20.

items.speaker: So he said
items.text: “How about, becaus e we have to live in New Zealand for 20 years, the
compensation for that is not to scrap the 5 years since 50, but” —he was actually
saying—“why do we not recognise that if you spend 5 years from 50 in the Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau, because they are R ealms of New Zealand, that qualifies
you?”. Because the reality is that they may have lived in other parts of the world. They
may have lived in Australia, or in Sweden, or in London, or wherever. So, actually, it
was about recognising people who come back to the Cook Islands and contribute to
those countries. And I think that has been the main contention.
When you look at all the statistics about how expensive it is, it actually does not
stack up. Currently 220 people receive New Zealand superannuation in t he Cook
Islands. That is about 33 percent of those who are eligible. When this legislation goes
through tonight, 245 people will become eligible. So there is not going to be a big flood.
The Government is not going to take a big hit. It is not going to cos t the Government a
lot of money. In fact, they have estimated that there will be an extra 16 people per
annum. So this is not about money. Yes, this is about the special status that the Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau have in New Zealand’s constitution, and about our
recognition that they are part of our country. They have automatic citizenship.
We would have contended that the Government could go just that little bit further
and got rid of the requirement. I think that in the Government’s mind Cook Island ers
live in New Zealand and then when they are 55, they leave here and go back to the
Cook Islands. The reality is that that is not what happens. So thank you to the people
who made a submission and thank you to the people who have contributed to the
debate. I commend the bill to the House, but with that caveat. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: It is with great pleasure that I rise to talk about the
Social Assistance (Portability to Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill. As a relatively
new MP I was reflecting today that I think this is the first bill where I have been a part
of the first reading, the Committee stage, the select committee, and seeing this through
to the end.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Not working hard enough.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: No, it is just a great thing for me to be able to be a part of. It is a
great thing to be able to be a part of doing something that is actually very positive. Of
course, everything this Government does is positive, and this is just another one of those
things. But it is just, I think, for me, something that we can really look at and say that
this is something positive we are doing for the people of the Cook Islands, Tokelau, and
Niue. I think the last speaker, Louisa Wall, summed it up when she reflected on the very
positive response that we had, in large part, from the submitters from those islands, who
talked about the fact that they were very grateful for what is going on here and what is
happening.
What we are doing is ensuring —and I think this is the particularly important part of
this—that people no longer have to be resident in New Zealand at the time at which
they apply for their superannuation to be able to be transferred to them if they are l iving
in any of these Realm of New Zealand Islands. I think it is a critical thing, because
people do sometimes want to go back a little earlier than the age of 65 to retire, and so it
is great that they can do that.
4602 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
I think what is critical about this, though, is that it actually gives people who are
from those places the same rights that are afforded to the rest of the New Zealanders
who are living here. I am 48 years old now. If at some time I decide that I want to move
to the Cook Islands or Niue or Tokelau and I want to stay there when I retire, I am
going to have to spend 5 years after the age of 50 in New Zealand. And yet what is
being proposed by Supplementary Order Paper 71, which has come from the other side
of the House, is to give people who are  from these i slands something that other New
Zealanders are not eligible for. That is not necessarily fair. So what we have done in
putting this legislation forward —despite the fact that a member over the other side
thought that not a lot of consideration had not gone into this, a huge amount of
consideration has gone into this to ensure that people can go back before the age of 65
and they can receive superannuation in exactly the same way as other New Zealanders
can. I think that is absolutely critical.
One of the points that was made from the other side of the House was just bizarre. I
just want to pick up on it, because it was stated that almost all of the submissions were
for changing this. I thought: you know what? If this Government —if any Government,
to be honest —said, every time that submissions came to a select committee, “Oh, the
people who came to make submissions asked for this so therefore we should give it to
them.”, well, the Government would go broke so quickly it would be unbelievable. So,
yes, we do need to listen to submissions, but we need to weigh them up against the
reality of the situation. Yes, we will get submissions on bills, but we do need to be sure
that we weigh those up against the reality of the situation. We listened to those people
and we have responded to those people, but it does not mean that we always have to do
just what somebody wants every time they ask.
These islands are facing some real issues. They are facing issues of depopulation.
They are facing some challenges. As a nation, New Zealand is offering protection to
those other islands in the Realm of New Zealand, and it is our responsibility to do what
we can in an appropriate way to assist them. That is exactly what we are doing through
this legislation. Through thi s legislation we are ensuring that it will be much easier for
people to go back, to be able to retire somewhere along the line, perhaps a little bit
earlier than they might have before, and to make some useful contribution back home in
those islands.
I have heard members on the other side use the word “mean”. They have used the
word “mean”. They have said that this Government is mean because we are not
changing—
Su’a William Sio: Mean-spirited,

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Mean -spirited, even, was the word that I have heard. It is
absolutely bizarre, because what we are talking about doing today is offering something
that has not been offered before —something that, up until now, has been missing,
through successive Governments of New Zealand. I do not want to lay blame, but it has
not been addressed until now. We are addressing it and we are doing it so that the
people of those Islands are being treated in the same way as any other New Zealander in
terms of whether they wan ted to retire there, and I think that is critical in what we are
doing.
So I want to finish up by saying we are committed to these i slands of the Realm of
New Zealand. We do take it very seriously. We do acknowledge the special place that
they do have, but we do need to make sure that what we do is fair, is equitable, and is in
line with everything else that we are doing. That is exactly what this bill does. This bill
ensures that we are working in a way that is most appropriate to meet the needs of those
islands and also keeping in mind what is fair and equitable for other New Zealanders.
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4603
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour —Māngere): I think that members of the Pacific
Islands listening in to this debate will have a very strong difficulty accepting or
believing the comments about this Government being committed to the Pacific. They
have heard it often—too often—and particularly in the last campaign, and it has all
come to naught. It means nothing. W ords are quite cheap. They have learnt to
understand and accept that this Government will say anything to try to bring people
around to its thinking, but at the end of the day they are just simply words.
I want to firstly acknowledge the leaders and the people of the community of the
Cook Islands who are listening in—kia orana tatou katoatoa. I also want to
acknowledge the leaders and people who are listening in from Niue, that place that we
affectionately call “the Rock”—fakalofa lahi atu. I also want to acknowledge the leaders
and people of Tokelau, who are prayerfully listening to this debate as well as
prayerfully waiting for one of their former Ulus who is sick in America, the honourable
Toloa. I acknowledge them because I am aware they have been listening in to the debate
as this piece of legislation goes through its passage in this House.
May I begin by saying that I want to share a Samoan saying: “ O e e lavea’i ia te a’u i
taimi o puapuaga, o ivi, o toto, o aano.” If I translated that, it would mean : “They who
come to my hour of need are my family. They are blood, bones, and flesh.” I say that at
the outset because when it comes to dealing with the Pacific, you are dealing with
people, and relationships are paramount in our ongoing dealings with the Pacific.
I have got just a few points that I want to raise. Firstly, I want to acknowledge Poto
Williams, Carmel Sepuloni, and members of New Zealand First and the Green Party.
We have stood united in acknowledging the fact that, yes, we support this bill , but we
believe that New Zealanders should be treated equally, regardless of where they are
based, and we support the removal of the 5- year resident and present status. I will tell
you why. New Zealand prides itself on saying that we have this constitutional
arrangement between New Zealand and members of the Realm countries: the Cook
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. Because we do not have a written constitution, we rely on
the words of past and present Prime Ministers, past and present Ministers of Foreign
Affairs, and past and present Governors-General.
For me, the Governor-General who enforced how important that was, was Sir Anand
Satyanand, who, everywhere he lived, walked, and spoke, would always acknowledge
the languages of the Realm of New Zealand: Māori,  English, sign language, Cook
Islands, Niuean, and Tokelauan. That says it all —that that Governor -General
acknowledged this uniquely special relationship. What does it mean? Time and time
again, Murray McCully and the Prime Minister, John Key, always say t his phrase: “We
New Zealanders have a special relationship with the Pacific.” But in their hour of need,
when the leaders of those countries present themselves at the select committee, what do
we give them? We give them half a pie, but we hold on to the other half. What for?

items.speaker: That reminds me of another Samoan saying
items.text: “ E u’u le afa, ae togi le moa. E togi le
moa ae u’u le afa. ” It is a trap. We will give you a little bit now, but we will hold on to
this other part for later on. If the relationship is importa nt, the Government should
recognise that these leaders come armed with the prayers and with the endorsement of
the people of those countries. They are New Zealand citizens. Why does this
Government continue to treat them as second -class citizens? Why is th at? That is what
it is doing. That is exactly what it is doing.
We had the Premier of Niue, the Prime Minister of the Cook Islands, and some
significant individuals from these countries come to make submissions. I want to read
something out that is import ant to me: “The unique and special relationship has seen
many New Zealand citizens move from the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau to work in
New Zealand and contribute economically, socially and culturally to [the] fabric of New
4604 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015
Zealand society.” That side o f the House —that Government—makes out as if we are
giving them a handout. That is what it believes. Here we have the Government of the
Cook Islands saying it is not a one -way street. Yes, they receive aid from New Zealand.
They have to. It is a constitutional obligation.
But by the same token, the people of the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau come here
and work, they go to school here, and they pay taxes here —they contribute. The Hon
Nandi Glassie lived in Māngere and worked in Manukau in local government until he
was about—oh, I do not know; he looks older now—I think around his 40s. He left here
and is now a Minister in the Cook Islands Government. So what do we tell him? When
he retires, he will not be eligible —he will not be eligible, because he has to be present
here in the land of Aotearoa New Zealand. But the land of Aotearoa New Zealand
should also include the Cook Islands —the soil, the land of the Cook Islands, Niue, and
Tokelau.
I agree with what my colleagues here on this side of the House have s aid. This
Government’s members are just being mean. They say words to the effect that the
relationship is real and genuine, but, in reality, these actions speak louder than the
words they continue to roll out.
Only yesterday Adrian Rurawhe, Kris Faafoi, J enny Salesa, and I attended Jerry
Collins’ funeral in Porirua. This is important. Peseta was there, and we helped him get
into the row we were sitting in because he did not want to sit next to Ken Douglas. We
were there. Prior to the funeral, we made a bri ef presentation to the family of Jerry
Collins in accordance with Samoan protocol and culture, to pay our respects, to convey
our alofas to them. The essence of all the testimonies and tributes made at that funeral
was that Jerry Collins never forgot where  he came from. Jerry Collins never forgot his
tupuaga—the people who supported him to the role that he played. Jerry Collins never
forgot his si’osi’omaga —his environment, what made him the person he was. He was
constantly working to give something back to “P-Town” or to the people who made him
the person he was and helped him along to become a star All Black. It was an amazing
funeral, and it was an amazing atmosphere—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!
Su’a WILLIAM SIO : —with all the tributes. I am getting to the point. The point I
am making, and this is with reference to the chairman of the Social Services Committee,
Alfred Ngaro, is that I want to appeal to him. When we were campaignin g last year, he
went out to the community and made promise after promise after promise in the
likeness of John Key to the people of the Pacific that if National came into Government,
things would happen—things would happen. I want to say to him that the si gn of a
Government that has become arrogant and drunk with its own mightiness is that it
refuses to listen to the people. I want to appeal to you, Alfred. You need to listen to the
people who helped you arrive at where you are now. This is important.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta Sam Lotu -Iiga
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This member has
been here long enough to know that he is getting well away—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. No, I am the judge of these
matters, and I am calling Su’a William Sio.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO: I am appealing to the chair of the Social Services Committee,
who heard the submissions, who heard the pleas from the Cook Islands Prime  Minister,
from the Premier of Tokelau, and from the elders of those communities —the
community that he belongs to. I am appealing to you: listen to the people. Do not live
up to the meaning of your name and forget who brought you to where you are.

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Assistant Speaker. That member knows
that there is an offence culturally to actually start to use a person’s name, which we
would never do. So I take offence, actually, at the use of that comment.
18 Jun 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 4605

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: All right, thank you. The member
has taken offence, and I ask the member who is speaking to withdraw that comment.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO: I withdraw. I appeal again to the chairman, Mr Alfred Ngaro.
Do not forget your tupuaga —the people who supported you, who covered you, who
enabled you to sit at the head of the table. Li sten to the pleas that they have given you,
because I am afraid that if you have not listened to their appeals and to their submission
to be flexible in your stance on this particular issue, then it means that you are selling
your soul. You are selling your soul, and that is a bad thing because there are so many
of us—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry to interrupt the honourable
member. The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I rise and take the final call on the third reading of
the Social Assistance (Portability to Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill. I want to
make reference to the comments that were made by Mr Sio and, in particul ar, when he
talked about actions speaking louder than words. Can I remind the member that in 1990
what was then the Social Welfare (Transitional Provisions) Act actually indicated that
you needed to have 7 years rather than 5 years. The year was changed so that it was 5
years to make it a lot more equitable. Can I remind that member that the Green member
who spoke, Jan Logie, also talked about how the petition for change for the provision of
the portability of the pension has been happening since 1990. So i f we are going to talk
about actions speaking louder than words, why when Labour was in Government were
there no changes made? I tell you the reason why: actions speak louder than words.
Here we are, with the honourable Minister Murray McCully putting acti ons to his
words. And, actually, under this Government, we are making it happen. Since 1990 the
petition has been happening.
If we talk about actions speaking louder than words, let us also talk to our Cook
Island, Niuean, and Tokelauan communities that a re out there. In the inquiry that was
taken in 2010 into New Zealand’s relationship with South Pacific nations, one of the
issues that it talked about was the Pacific Parliamentary and Political Leaders Forum.
Now, the member Mr Sio will know that this is not a new issue. In fact, when Mike
Moore was in Parliament he talked about it. When Helen Clark was in Parliament she
talked about it. But guess what happened? Under that Government —when Labour was
in Government—nothing happened. So what happened? Minister McCully turned round
and in 2013 we had the very first Pacific Parliamentary and Political Leaders Forum,
with 138 members from across the Pacific. They came here and, for the first time, we
talked about issues that affect our Pacific nations. When actio ns speak louder than
words, it is under this Government that we make it happen.
The last thing —because it is good to have a trifecta —when we talk about actions
speaking louder than words is that it was under a Labour Government that the Pacific
Island aff airs portfolio was taken out of Cabinet for the very first time. The Pacific
community turned round and asked: “Why? Why did this happen?”. It was under a
Labour Government and those people could not understand it. Why? Because, for all the
talk and for al l the rhetoric, that Government was not appealing to the so- called
submissions of the Pacific community. [ Interruption] No, I do not stand to take those
comments; I stand to actually proclaim the things that this Government has done. It is
making a difference.
I am going to round off my speech with just a few comments that I think are actually
really important to actually address some of the issues of concern. I want to address the
issue that Louisa Wall raised when she talked about discrimination. I am going to read
this out really clearly: some members have also said that it is unfair that migrants can
come to New Zealand and qualify for full New Zealand superannuation—

items.speaker: Louisa Wall
items.text: I didn’t say that.
4606 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 18 Jun 2015

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: —no, no, no, I am just reading from this—

items.speaker: Louisa Wall
items.text: After 10 years—after 10 years.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: —hang on, let me finish, OK —residence in New Zealand,
whereas people who live in the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau must have 20 years’
residence. That is the point I wanted to make —the 20 years’ residence. This bill does
not discriminate against people from the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau. People from
these islands who remain in New Zealand are subject to exactly the same rules as all
other New Zealanders. I want to make that point really clear to all other New
Zealanders. There has been a lot of misinformation that has gone out to our community
to believe that there is discrimination and that there is an injustice. Absolutely there is
not. What you are talking about is the special portability provisions that are there as
well. I want to be very clear. These provisions that are there are absolutely important.
They do allow for the migration back into the Pacific, which is what the communi ties
have asked for. If we are talking about what they have asked for, Mr Sio, this is what
they have asked for —those Pacific nations, those Pacific leaders. When they came and
they presented they said: “These are the things that we have been waiting for —these are
the things that we have been waiting for for a very long time.” So this Government put
actions to the words and is making it happen.
The last thing is around this 5- year rule. You are absolutely right, Mr Darroch Ball:
12 out of the 13 submissions said: “Can we find that there is some discretion around
that?”. There is no discretion for anybody. When we talk about those who have
discretion, you are right that there are those for whom there is a social security
agreement, a reciprocal financial arrangement, that is made with those particular nations
like the UK, like Canada, and like Australia, and that is that arrangement. There is no
discrimination there at all. Therefore all New Zealanders, all Cook Islanders, all Niuean
people, and all Tokelauan people have exactly the same.
I want to finish off by saying this. This is a bill that is ensuring that when the
community of the Pacific has asked for portability of that pension they shall receive it.
They will be able to go back, and when they go back at the age of 55 —my parents are
residing back in the Cook Islands as we speak, and they are there now. When we are
asked for the reasons why, these are the reasons why: it allows for them to return back,
to give back to their local economies, so that depopulation, where they are migrating
out, does not happen. They return back and they can give something back to those local
economies.
This is a good bill. It is a bill that we know, right across the House, has added
support, bar one point of difference. We  have justified that, we know what that is, and,
you are absolutely right, it will impact 245 people every year, increasing by about a
hundred people who can make the application. We know that that is there. But we know
that actually it is clear. The provisions of the bill make the difference.
Lastly, I want to finish with this. There were some comments made by New Zealand
First and its leader that there were promises made back in the Cook Islands by Andrew
Bayly and by me at the Swordfish Club or Swordfighters Bar, whatever it is. There were
absolutely no promises that were made—no promises that were made. The only promise
that was made was this: that we would address the issue of the 5 years. I can say with
hand on heart that the only promise that was mad e was to address the issue of 5 years,
not to fix or change that.
I am proud of this bill. I am married to my beautiful wife, Mokauina Fuemana -
Ngaro, who is Samoan and Niuean and comes from the beautiful village of Mutalau in
Niue. I am of Cook Island descent, and I am proud that this bill will make a difference. I
commend this bill, in its third reading, to the House.
Bill read a third time.
18 Jun 2015 EEZ & Cont. Shelf (Enviro. Effects) (Trans. Prov.) Amdt Bill 4607

sections.heading: Exclusive Economic Zone And Continental Shelf

items.text: (ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS) (TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS)
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I move, That the
Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) (Transitional
Provisions) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . This bill deals with the exclusive
economic zone, which amounts to an area 21 times the area of New Z ealand’s land
mass. Prior to 2012 there was no environmental assessment of oil platforms, minerals
activities, or the like in that massive area of space, and I am proud to be part of a
Government that has actually provided for a robust system of scrutiny f or activities that
might take place in that area. But we have the issue of the four major platforms of
activities that occur in that space and how we might transition them into the new
regime. There are four operators: Shell Todd Oil Services, with the Māui platform;
Australian Worldwide Exploration, which runs the Tūī platform; OMV New Zealand,
on the Maari platform; and Origin Energy Resources, with the Kupe platform. The
regime we put in place required each of those to apply to the Environmental Protecti on
Authority for a consent at the time their minerals permit expired. Shell Todd Oil
Services was the first of those to come up for renewal in respect of its minerals permit
and it properly applied for a permit and consent from the Environmental Protection
Authority, and that consent has now been granted.
The issue that is before the Parliament with this bill is that in the event that anybody
chooses to appeal that consent, we could have the quite unsatisfactory position, after the
end of this month, where  Shell Todd Oil Services would not be able to continue to use
that platform at Māui and, as a consequence, there would be a significant effect on the
security of 20 percent of the gas supply for New Zealand. What this bill simply makes
plain is that in the  event that that decision is appealed, Shell Todd Oil Services can
continue to use the consent and that platform through to the date when all of the appeal
processes are concluded, and I would be very surprised if there was any member of this
House who would logically take issue with that. Of course we also deal with the other
three operators by clearly setting out the process when they come to apply through the
same process.
I want to commend the work the Local Government and Environment Committee
did, and I commend the work of the Committee of the whole House, which finalised this
bill. A future reapplication will now be required over a period of 9 months. The
technical amendments that have been made through the select committee process clarify
the way in  which the Environmental Protection Authority will deal with those
applications. With these additional transitional provisions we will end up with a sensible
regime in which we can bring those previous permits in when we did not have a regime
for the assessment of environmental effects for those applications previously made. It is
a sensible bill. It is a bill that provides for the continuation of New Zealand’s central
energy supplies while also ensuring that we have integrity for the Environmental
Protection Authority’s assessment of those environmental effects and the conditions that
it has recommended in its decision around the continuation of the Māui platform. For all
those reasons I commend the bill to the House.
Debate interrupted.
